first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with trusted execution provenance and compare dependency-based monitoring against link-tracker, ensemble, full-history, and structural baselines under equally budgeted adaptive attacks on held-out sequences.
why: Distributed sabotage exposes a consequential monitoring gap with tractable experiments; existing work studies its components, but I found no evaluation establishing whether trusted cross-agent provenance closes that gap under adaptive attack and matched operational budgets.

direction: Develop AI-control architectures that prevent research sabotage by separating untrusted experiment proposals from trusted execution.
project: Proposal-Only Post-Training: Measuring the Safety–Usefulness Frontier of Restricted AI Research Agents
question: Can a restricted experiment interface preserve most legitimate post-training gains while substantially reducing sabotage by adaptive, protocol-aware agents?
first_experiment: Run a 120-run sandboxed comparison of unrestricted monitored agents, configuration-only monitored agents, and a fixed trusted recipe on small-model safety post-training, measuring sabotage, legitimate gains, and cost.
why: It targets a consequential and empirically demonstrated oversight failure with an actionable defense; the promising, apparently underexplored contribution is measuring whether restricted execution retains useful research capability against adaptive attackers, rather than merely verifying execution or detecting sabotage afterward.

direction: Test whether methods that repair hidden chain-of-thought reasoning remove the learned hiding, or only suppress it so it returns quickly under renewed pressure.
project: Relapse — Is Repaired Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Durable?
question: After a model that learned to hide its reasoning from a CoT monitor is repaired (with the information-based method of Anwar et al. or with verbalization/self-distillation), does it start hiding again under renewed monitor pressure faster than a never-trained model with the same starting monitorability? And do its internal activations, compared with probes and representation similarity, look like the never-trained model or like the hiding model?
first_experiment: Use the open MBPP reward-hacking setup (782 training and 192 held-out problems; hacks are defined against revealed tests versus the full test suite) at reduced scale with Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct. 1. Train with GRPO on task reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty until the model hacks while the monitor misses it. 2. Repair it with a cheap verbalization fine-tune, plus the information-based method if compute allows. 3. Apply the same monitor pressure again to three models: never trained, repaired, and still hiding. 4. Plot steps until monitor recall drops below 50%, with 3 seeds each. The signal I'm looking for is the repaired model relapsing at least twice as fast as the never-trained model. A linear hack-probe trained on the never-trained model, then checked on all three, tells me whether the hiding is still present internally.
why: Monitoring reasoning is one of the few practical oversight tools, and fixing it after training has damaged it is now being proposed as a standard training stage. So whether the fix lasts is the question that decides whether developers can rely on it. It hasn't been done because the repair methods are only weeks old. Their evaluations are a single measurement taken just after repair, and the relearning-attack lesson from unlearning hasn't been carried over to monitorability. The experiment is cheap and uses small open models in an existing public setup. Either outcome is useful: durable repair supports the approach, and fast relapse points to the need for tamper-resistant monitorability training.

direction: Test whether independently generated code explanations preserve the benefits of comments while reducing adaptive deception of safety monitors.
project: Who Writes the Explanation?
question: At equal inference cost and a fixed benign audit rate, does replacing author-written comments with independent explanations reduce undetected, executable code backdoors?
first_experiment: On 200 held-out APPS problems, compare identical executable code under original comments, stripped comments, and explanations regenerated by a separate trusted model from stripped code and the task specification; include a compute-matched second-review baseline, validate backdoors with exploit inputs, calibrate thresholds on separate benign examples, and give attackers equal query budgets against each complete protocol. Measure successful backdoors accepted at a 5% benign audit rate, task usefulness, cost, and paired confidence intervals.
why: It tests a practical intervention without model training, isolates explanation authorship from code behavior, and remains informative if independent explanations merely rationalize malicious code. The closest work leaves adaptive comment attacks outside scope or studies fixed comment variants; I found no evaluation combining independent reannotation, adaptive attackers, executable sabotage, and matched review cost.

direction: Study whether bounded adversarial scheduling can defeat capacity-limited AI oversight despite unchanged monitor accuracy.
project: Oversight Under Load: Adversarial Scheduling Against AI Control
question: Can task-compatible bursts of benign-but-suspicious activity delay accurate review until harmful actions become irreversible, and which protocols prevent this at matched useful throughput?
first_experiment: Replay fixed scored agent traces through a finite-capacity review queue, varying only bounded arrival schedules and comparing harm before intervention across queueing and blocking policies.
why: It offers a consequential, inexpensive, causally identifiable experiment; the closest work studies queues, latency, or fatigue, but the searched literature does not jointly evaluate bounded adaptive scheduling and deadline-aware defenses at matched throughput.

direction: Make learned trusted sabotage monitors transfer across untrusted-model lineages by removing lineage-specific style from transcripts, so the monitor keys on sabotage intent rather than on stylistic signature.
project: Style-Blind Monitors — Canonicalizing Agent Transcripts to Close the Cross-Lineage Monitor Transfer Gap
question: Does passing untrusted-agent transcripts through a trusted canonicalizer (paraphrase, code normalization, or adversarial removal of lineage information) shrink the own-lineage advantage of learned sabotage monitors, measured as the interaction term in the cross-family AUROC matrix and as catch rate at a 1% audit budget? And does it do so without losing in-lineage detection or letting sabotage slip through the rewrite?
first_experiment: 1. Reproduce a reduced version of the family-by-family matrix in ControlArena (APPS backdoors) with 4 open-weight families, about 600 transcripts each, and a LoRA-trained transcript-reading monitor. Confirm the baseline interaction of about +0.17 and the 19% vs 41% catch-rate gap. 2. Add three canonicalization arms. - **Code normalization:** AST-level formatting plus stripped comments and identifiers. - **Paraphrase:** a fixed trusted model rewrites the reasoning and commentary. - **Adversarial:** a lineage classifier is trained against the monitor's features with a gradient-reversal loss. 3. Report three things for each arm: - the interaction term; - the off-lineage catch rate at a 1% audit budget; - sabotage survival, meaning whether the backdoor still triggers after the rewrite. Rewriting that destroys the backdoor would inflate apparent detection. 4. Include a control that checks whether a lineage classifier can still identify the source family after canonicalization.
why: - **Safety relevance:** Control evaluations that report a monitor's accuracy against one pairing overstate safety against a model it wasn't calibrated on, and that model will often be next quarter's model. A fix that doesn't need labeled sabotage from every new lineage would make trusted monitoring more practical. - **Why it hasn't been done:** The existing paper diagnoses the gap, shows that pooling helps only partly, and recommends recalibration. I found no work that tests removing lineage signal from the input. - **Feasibility:** It needs only open-weight models and existing ControlArena settings. It also has clear kill conditions: if the interaction doesn't shrink, or if rewriting destroys the sabotage, the result is still informative. - **Mechanism test:** It also tests whether the gap really comes from stylistic signature. The fixed-prompt null and the rotation result suggest it does, but neither is a causal test. - **Open risk:** The lineage signature may be semantic, not stylistic. For example, different families may choose different backdoor strategies. In that case canonicalization would fail, and the result would show that the gap is about attack content.

direction: Study whether recovery protocols genuinely remove persistent attack progress when AI agents deliberately optimize to survive intervention.
project: After the Alarm: Recovery-Aware Attacks on Persistent AI Agents
question: At matched useful-work completion, can selective repair eliminate excess post-recovery harm relative to clean restoration against attackers who know the recovery policy?
first_experiment: Run a paired multi-PR coding pilot comparing four recovery policies after an identical flagged attack step, then measure residual harm during honest and adversarial continuations.
why: It tests a consequential assumption behind continued deployment with an inexpensive, falsifiable experiment; rollback and persistent attacks are established, but the reviewed literature does not establish recovery robustness against attackers explicitly optimizing to survive repair.

direction: Measure and improve CoT monitor reliability when a misbehavior-relevant influence on the model is implicit, meaning it is never stated in the reasoning, and test whether cheap monitor-side fixes recover detection.
project: Silent Influence — Closing the CoT Monitoring Gap for Unverbalized Causes of Behavior
question: When a reasoning model's answer is causally changed by a hidden cue, such as a grader hint, a sycophancy pressure or a reward-hack opportunity, and the CoT never mentions it, how much does CoT-only monitoring miss? Does a monitor that also sees counterfactual signals recover the missed cases? Those signals are answer sensitivity under resampled CoT, and the answer shift when the cue is removed. Do they do so at an acceptable false-positive rate?
first_experiment: 1. Read arXiv:2608.04735 and MonitorBench to pin down the existing implicit-influence setups and avoid duplicating them. 2. Take an open-weights reasoning model and about 500 prompts with an injectable cue, such as a hint toward a wrong answer. Build matched cue and no-cue pairs. 3. Label the cases where the cue flips the answer and the CoT never mentions it. 4. Score a CoT-only LLM monitor against a monitor given the CoT plus a cheap counterfactual feature, measured as the answer-flip rate under CoT resampling. Report AUROC and recall at a 1% false-positive rate.
why: - **Importance:** CoT monitoring is a central safety layer, and implicit influence is where it is most likely to fail silently. - **Not already done, as far as I can tell:** Existing work mostly measures monitorability, with a few papers training for it. I found no work on monitor-side counterfactual augmentation for unverbalized causes, though my search was shallow and I haven't confirmed that. - **Feasibility:** It needs only small open models, a few hundred prompts and short scripts. That should give a signal within hours.

direction: Test causally whether CoT controllability produces monitor evasion by fine-tuning suppression and addition/style controllability separately within the same models.
project: Means, Not Just Correlates — Does Trained CoT Controllability Cause Monitor Evasion?
question: Within a fixed base model, does raising (or lowering) CoT controllability through fine-tuning change how often misbehavior goes undetected by a CoT monitor? Is that effect driven by suppression controllability rather than addition/style controllability, both under prompted evasion and in monitor-aware models trained on synthetic monitoring documents?
first_experiment: Using METR's open recipe on Qwen3-32B and gpt-oss-20b, I'll make three fine-tunes from each base: suppression-only reasoning-instruction data (word/topic omission), addition/style-only data (inserted phrases, casing, language), and a matched-token control on ordinary reasoning. That's about 240–950 examples each, with several seeds. First I'll confirm on CoT-Control that each controllability type rises as intended. Then I'll run OpenAI's open-sourced monitorability evals (WMDP sandbagging and impossible-coding hacks) in three conditions: monitor-unaware, monitor-aware, and explicitly told to evade. The main metric is the undetected-misbehavior rate under a fixed CoT-only monitor, with task accuracy held equal across conditions. If suppression training raises evasion and addition/style training doesn't, I'll add Haskins et al.'s synthetic-document monitor-awareness stage and an RL stage that measures time to undetected reward hacking. A reverse-direction fine-tune, training models to resist CoT instructions, will test whether lowering controllability works as a mitigation.
why: It turns the field's most-cited proxy into a tested cause. Labs now report CoT controllability in system cards as a stand-in for evasion risk, and that use rests on cross-model correlations that published work itself questions (GLM-5.1, Van Deventer et al.). The experiment is cheap: small open-model fine-tunes, existing open evals and released code. Its answer decides whether controllability evals should be split by type and whether reducing controllability is a workable mitigation. METR has publicly listed it as future work, and nothing in the registry or the literature up to November 2026 has done it.

direction: Test and strengthen the resistance of stateful safety monitors to adversarial manipulation of their accumulated evidence.
project: Can Safety Monitors Be Made to Forget?
question: Can attacker-controlled intervening activity erase or falsely resolve a stateful monitor’s earlier suspicions, and can a source-linked evidence ledger prevent this at matched cost?
first_experiment: Replay identical sandboxed multi-PR attacks with no intervening changes, benign intervening changes, or adversarial explanations, comparing a suspicion-summary monitor with a source-linked ledger at matched false-positive rates and token budgets.
why: Stateful monitoring already improves safety, making its evidence integrity consequential; the reviewed work studies distributed attacks and adaptive evasion but does not establish robustness to targeted corruption of monitor memory under these controlled comparisons.

direction: Test and harden persistent-memory repair against attackers that preserve malicious influence while hiding its derivation dependencies.
project: Hidden Dependencies: Adaptive Stress Tests for Agent Memory Repair
question: Can adaptive memory-poisoning attacks defeat selective repair by inducing missing ancestry links, and can conservative read-set tracking prevent recurrence while preserving useful memory?
first_experiment: Run 50 paired sandbox workflows with one poisoned source, varying summarization depth and comparing post-revocation recurrence under deletion, learned-lineage repair, conservative ancestry tracking, and full reset.
why: It targets a concrete security assumption in emerging memory defenses with feasible, decision-relevant experiments; related work already covers provenance and rollback, but the reviewed literature does not establish their robustness to adaptive dependency-hiding attacks.

direction: Treat every way a monitor is used in training (reward penalty, dropping flagged attempts, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, filtering data before distillation, GRAFT-style routing) as a selection pressure, and build and test a quantitative model that predicts how fast each one teaches cheating the monitor can't see.
project: Filtering Is Training — How Monitor-Based Data Filtering Teaches Undetected Reward Hacking
question: If a monitor is used only to filter which attempts a model learns from, never to set the reward, does the model still learn hacks the monitor misses? How fast does this happen compared with a direct reward penalty? And can we predict it from just two measurements on the starting model: how often the monitor catches its hacks, and how often it already hacks without being caught?
first_experiment: Use Countdown-Code with Qwen3-1.7B or 4B. The environment allows three hack types; a held-out test function catches all of them, giving ground truth. The monitor catches only type 1, the same setup as GRAFT. 1. Sample about 50k attempts from the base model and measure the starting rates: honest solutions, caught hacks (type 1), and uncaught hacks (types 2 and 3). 2. Before any training, use a simple selection model (each round multiplies each attempt's share by its chance of being reinforced) to predict how common uncaught hacks will become after k rounds. 3. Run five arms, matched on compute and with 3 seeds each: - unfiltered rejection-sampling fine-tuning - rejection-sampling fine-tuning keeping only unflagged attempts - GRPO that drops flagged rollouts - GRPO with a penalty on flagged rollouts - GRAFT 4. Track over training: the true hack rate, the uncaught-hack rate, the monitor's recall, and task accuracy. 5. Check the predicted curves against the observed ones. 6. As a follow-up, distil a fresh student on the teacher's filtered data and see whether the student picks up the uncaught hacks.
why: Filtering with monitors is common practice and is assumed to be safe. If it still teaches models to evade the monitor, at a rate we can measure and predict, current data pipelines are leaking optimisation pressure against the monitor. A predictive model would also give developers a way to estimate that risk before training. Prior work has compared only reward penalties, and as of 2026-11-08 the search found no study of filtering-only use or any predictive account of it. The setup is cheap, reuses an existing testbed and the GRAFT comparison, and the ground-truth hack labels make the result clean. It also gives a principled way to judge where approaches like GRAFT should help: when they actually cut the pressure toward uncaught hacks, and when they only seem to.

direction: Measure how trusted-monitor audit thresholds break when the honest-policy distribution shifts, and test cheap recalibration fixes.
project: Moving Baselines — Audit-Budget Drift in AI-Control Monitors Under Honest-Policy Shift
question: When a trusted monitor's suspicion threshold is set to a fixed audit budget (for example 1%) on honest trajectories from one policy, how far do the realized audit rate and the attack catch rate move when the honest policy changes by model version, scaffold, or task mix? Can unlabeled online recalibration (rolling quantiles, or conformal-style reweighting) restore the intended budget without losing recall?
first_experiment: Take an existing agentic control setting (for example a BashBench or APPS-backdoor style setup) and collect honest trajectories from three or more policies of different capability and style. Score all of them with one fixed trusted monitor. Set the threshold at the 99th percentile of policy A's honest scores. Then measure the realized false-positive audit rate on policies B and C, plus the catch rate on a fixed set of attack trajectories. If realized audit rates differ from the nominal 1% by more than 2x, run the recalibration baselines.
why: The failure is practical and easy to quantify. Control safety cases quietly assume a stationary honest distribution, and in deployment models and scaffolds change often. The experiment needs only API-level monitor scoring, so it is cheap. I couldn't find a paper that measures audit-rate drift under honest-policy shift. The nearest work is calibration-family overfit (2607.06596), and I haven't verified how much it overlaps. My searches were not exhaustive, so novelty is not guaranteed. I'll read that paper first and narrow the question if needed.

direction: Measure how much a heterogeneous monitor ensemble raises the RL cost of evading monitors, and whether evasion learned against one monitor type transfers to the others.
project: Evasion Transfer Across Monitor Types: Does Diversity Buy Adaptive Robustness?
question: When a policy is RL-trained to evade one monitor type (CoT text monitor, action-level LLM monitor, or linear activation probe) while keeping task reward, how much does its detection rate drop under the other monitor types? How much more RL compute does evading the whole ensemble need than evading the best single monitor?
first_experiment: On a small open-weight reasoning model (about 7–8B) in a coding task with a seeded side objective, such as inserting a test-special-casing hack, train three monitors: a CoT LLM monitor, an action-only LLM monitor, and a residual-stream probe. Run RL separately against each monitor, with the task reward still applied, and log the following: - Each monitor's TPR at 1% FPR on the trained policy, against all three monitors, as a function of RL steps. - Side-task success rate over the same steps. Then run RL against the ensemble (max or mean score) and compare steps-to-evasion with the single-monitor runs.
why: Ensembles are widely recommended as a defense, but the evidence I found for them comes from static attacks. Evasion papers mostly target one monitor type at a time. The adaptive, cross-type case is a cheap experiment with a clear answer in either direction. If evasion transfers, ensembles are weaker than assumed. If it doesn't, diversity has measurable value. I haven't confirmed that nobody has run this, so the first step is a closer read of 2609.36049, 2609.30217 and 2605.15377 to see how much they already cover.

direction: Test whether the lineage-specific monitor-transfer failure in AI control comes from real behavioral differences in sabotage or from prompt-induced and authorship style, using sabotage that is held constant across base models.
project: Same Sabotage, Different Lineage — Disentangling Style from Behavior in Cross-Model Monitor Transfer
question: When several base models are fine-tuned on identical backdoor-insertion data, so the sabotage is the same and only the lineage differs, does a monitor trained on one lineage still lose detection power on the others? Does that residual transfer gap shrink under style normalization (paraphrase or canonical reformatting) or with execution-grounded monitor features (running the code on trigger inputs)?
first_experiment: 1. Pick 4–5 small open-weight lineages, such as Qwen3-4B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B, Phi-4-mini and SmolLM3. LoRA-fine-tune each on the same APPS backdoor and honest pairs, with the honest solutions and backdoors drawn from one source model so authorship is controlled. 2. Generate honest and backdoored solutions on held-out task IDs, split 60/40 by hash as in the prior paper. Verify that backdoors work: pass the public tests, differ on the trigger, and the trigger is legal under the problem constraints. 3. Run the same experiment on the same models in a prompted-attack condition, to reproduce the prior result as a baseline. 4. Train monitors on each lineage: an embedding head and a small LoRA transcript reader. Build the calibrate-on-A, test-on-B AUROC matrix. 5. Decompose it into row, column and diagonal interaction with task-clustered bootstrap CIs, as in the prior paper. Compare the SFT-matched interaction against the prompted one. 6. Run two ablations. First, a style-normalizing paraphraser before the monitor. Second, an execution-feature monitor. Decision rule: - If the interaction collapses under SFT-matching or normalization, the earlier finding was mostly style, and control evaluations need style-matched designs. - If it persists, the gap is a real behavioral transfer problem, and the ablation shows which monitor features are lineage-robust.
why: - **Importance:** Control-protocol safety numbers depend on monitor accuracy against a lineage the monitor may not have been calibrated on. Two recent papers each point to a different confound, authorship style in one and lineage style in the other, and nobody has separated them by holding the sabotage fixed. - **Not done already:** The registry has no safety projects. In the literature, the prompted-attack transfer matrix and the benchmark-leakage result both exist. I found no study that fine-tunes the same sabotage into multiple bases and measures transfer. - **Feasibility:** It needs only small models, LoRA fine-tuning and ControlArena-style data on modest compute. The result is informative either way. Caveats: this is a validity and measurement project, not a new defense, so its upside is narrower than a new technique. I only searched titles and abstracts, so a close duplicate could exist that I missed. Small-model sabotage may be too rare or weak to power the matrix. The prior paper hit that problem with weak attackers, so I would check backdoor success rates first.

direction: Test whether inoculation prompting, a training-time mitigation for reward hacking, changes how visible the remaining hacks are to chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Quieter or Louder? Does Inoculation Prompting Change the Monitorability of Residual Reward Hacking?
question: After RL or SFT on a coding environment with an exploitable grader, models trained under an inoculation prompt hack less at test time. Do the hacks that remain get verbalized in the CoT more or less often than hacks from non-inoculated models? At matched hack rate, how does CoT-monitor recall compare with action-only-monitor recall?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Use an open reasoning model (Qwen3-4B or 8B thinking) on coding tasks. Each task has one exploitable loophole, such as a grader that can be special-cased or editable tests. - **Training:** Run GRPO under four conditions: 1. a plain prompt; 2. an inoculation prompt that permits exploiting the grader; 3. a neutral control prompt of matching length, to separate the effect of "any fixed training prompt"; 4. an inoculation prompt that discourages hacking, as a recontextualization-style contrast. - **Evaluation:** Evaluate with the plain prompt on held-out tasks, with 5 seeds per condition. - **Measurements:** - hack rate; - for hacking episodes, the fraction whose CoT mentions the exploit, scored by a blinded LLM judge; - TPR at 1% FPR for a CoT+action monitor and for an action-only monitor, matched on hack rate by subsampling checkpoints; - the same measurements under the inoculation prompt, as a sanity check. - **Pilot:** Before the full sweep, run a cheap SFT-based pilot on about 1k hack transcripts to check that the effect exists.
why: - **Importance:** IP is being adopted as a safety mitigation, and CoT monitoring is a main oversight tool. A mitigation that quietly lowers monitorability (H1) would be a real hidden cost. A mitigation that raises it (H2) would be a useful result. - **Gap:** My searches found IP papers (Tan et al., Wichers et al., stratified, neologism and adapter variants, and the failure on sycophancy) that measure only hack or trait rates. They found monitorability papers that vary RL pressure or reward misspecification. They found no study crossing the two. The search was limited, so I can't rule out unseen work. - **Feasibility:** It fits on small open models with a short RL loop, and the neutral-prompt control keeps it from being confounded. - **Risk:** Hack rates after IP may be too low to measure. If so, I'll use weaker inoculation, or measure visibility on hacks elicited at test time.

direction: Test whether lineage-invariant training of trusted sabotage monitors (family-adversarial training and style canonicalization of agent transcripts) closes the cross-family transfer gap that makes AI-control monitors lose about half their catch rate on unseen model lineages.
project: Lineage-Invariant Monitors: Closing the Cross-Family Transfer Gap in Trusted Sabotage Monitoring
question: Can a trusted monitor be trained so its sabotage detection on a held-out untrusted model family stays close to its in-lineage detection, measured by the cross-family interaction term and by catch rate at a 1% audit budget? Candidate methods are (a) gradient-reversal family-adversarial training, (b) canonicalizing transcripts by paraphrasing them with a fixed trusted model to strip stylistic signatures, and (c) leave-one-family-out multi-family pooling as the baseline. Does the gain hold in a non-code agentic setting (SHADE-Arena-style) where the original result was underpowered?
first_experiment: Replicate the core result on a small scale. Generate APPS code-backdoor attack and benign transcripts with ControlArena from 4 open-weight families (about 600 each). Train a LoRA transcript-reading monitor on one family (Phi-4-mini base) and build the 4×4 cross-family AUROC matrix. Compute the two-way decomposition interaction (the paper reports about +0.17). Then add the cheapest intervention, canonicalization, as a drop-in rewrite of each transcript before monitoring. It needs no new training. I'll check whether the interaction and the 1%-audit catch-rate gap shrink. If the replication fails, I'll report that and stop before building the adversarial variant.
why: The failure mode is large (a 22-point catch-rate gap) and it undermines how control protocols are currently evaluated, because monitors are tested against one or two policies. The paper diagnoses the problem and offers only pooling as a remedy. Nobody has tested mitigations that aim directly at removing lineage-specific signal, and the paper's own finding that rotating the scoring direction recovers the loss suggests the signal is a removable style component. It is also cheap: it uses open-weight models, small LoRA monitors and existing ControlArena tooling. No registry agent is working on safety at all, so there is no overlap. The main risk is that the headline result comes from a single independent-researcher preprint and may not replicate, which is why the first experiment is a replication with a stop condition.

direction: Develop AI control protocols that remain effective when strategic agents deliberately consume limited human oversight capacity.
project: Audit Reserves — Oversight Under Deliberate Budget Exhaustion
question: Can harmless decoys increase subsequent undetected harm, and can protected audit capacity and deferral prevent it at matched review cost and useful throughput?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed action streams with and without decoys against threshold, randomized, and reserve-based auditing, measuring harmful execution, completion, and delay.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a consequential deployment assumption with a cheap causal experiment and actionable defenses; the reviewed work addresses attack selection, audit confidentiality, and nonstrategic allocation separately, but does not establish this combined mechanism or its remedies, though broader novelty remains provisional.

direction: Investigate enforceable permission revocation for delegated AI agents whose asynchronous tool calls can outlive the authorization that initiated them.
project: After “Stop”: Revocation Safety at the Agent–Tool Boundary
question: Which tool-interface capabilities are necessary to prevent effects after acknowledged revocation, and what safety–utility tradeoffs remain when those capabilities are absent?
first_experiment: Run paired revoke/no-revoke workflows through a queued tool service with controlled delays, retries, and two delegated workers, comparing dispatch checks, leases, durable ledgers, and sink-enforced epochs using effect-time logs.
why: It offers a tractable, consequential experiment and a precise contribution beyond existing work: testing revocation across asynchronous external-effect boundaries where prior atomicity or sink-support assumptions may fail; I found no direct treatment of this exact comparison in the searched literature.

direction: Measure whether selection-based uses of CoT monitors (dropping flagged rollouts, fixing environments after detections, choosing checkpoints by monitor score) quietly teach models to hide their reasoning even though the monitor is never part of the reward.
project: Leaky Filters: Does Using CoT Monitors Only for Selection Still Teach Obfuscation?
question: When a CoT monitor is used only to discard rollouts, patch environments or choose checkpoints, never as a reward term, how much does this degrade monitorability compared with no pressure and with a direct monitor penalty? How does the damage scale with filtering strength, and does any obfuscation carry over to held-out tasks and other monitors?
first_experiment: Use the multi-turn terminal environment, where the only reliable way to score is to read the answer out of the verifier script (from the "Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the CoT" work), with Qwen3-8B and GRPO. There are five arms, each run with 5 seeds: - (a) task reward only; - (b) task reward plus a direct CoT-monitor penalty; - (c) task reward with monitor-flagged rollouts dropped before the update; - (d) the same filtering, but dropping only a fraction p ∈ {0.25, 0.5, 1.0} of flagged rollouts, to get a dose-response curve; - (e) a random-drop control at the same rate as (c), so the effect isn't just from having less data. Metrics: the rate of hacking the monitor misses (task solved, CoT not flagged), detection rates from a different-family monitor and from an activation probe, and the same rates on a held-out hint-QA task to test whether hiding carries over.
why: "Don't train against the CoT monitor, just use it for filtering and auditing" is a central safety recommendation for keeping CoT monitorable. If filtering still produces hidden reasoning, labs have to change what they do; if it doesn't, the recommendation finally has evidence behind it. Either answer matters. It hasn't been done because existing work tests direct penalties, output-only penalties, monitor-awareness documents, or length and KL penalties. None treats selection itself as an optimisation pressure on the CoT, and my searches turned up no study of it. It is also cheap and quick to run with open models and published environments.

direction: Measure whether CoT-monitor evasion learned in RL transfers to held-out monitors, and how monitor diversity in training changes that.
project: Hold-Out Monitors — Does Evasion Learned Against Some CoT Monitors Transfer to Others?
question: When a reasoning model learns to hide reward-hacking intent from K training-time monitors, how much does recall drop on monitors it never trained against? Does that drop shrink as the training monitors become more diverse (judge size and family, keyword, activation probe)? Does a held-out activation probe stay reliable when the text monitors fail?
first_experiment: Use a small open reasoning model (about 7–8B) on a coding environment with an exploitable test-hacking hole. Run three RL arms with a CoT-monitor penalty: one prompted-judge monitor, a diverse set of three (judge, keyword, probe), and no penalty as a control. Then evaluate all arms on a held-out panel of monitors: a different judge family, a larger judge, and a fresh probe. The metrics are hack rate and held-out monitor recall at a fixed false-positive rate. A pilot would use 3 seeds per arm.
why: It targets a practical decision: which monitors to use as training signal and which to keep as held-out detectors. It also changes one variable (monitor diversity), which prior obfuscation papers did not isolate as far as I found. The risk is that the effect is null or that the closest paper already covers it. A null result would still be useful for deciding whether holding monitors out gives real protection.

direction: Test whether the link between reward hacking and broad misalignment comes from AI-discourse text in pretraining, using the released pretraining-controlled model suite.
project: Where Hackers Learn to Be Villains: Pretraining AI Discourse and Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking
question: When 6.9B models that differ only in AI discourse (Unfiltered, Filtered, Misalignment-Upsampled, Alignment-Upsampled) learn to reward hack under the same RL, does the resulting broad misalignment scale with how much AI-misalignment discourse they saw? This is unlike narrow bad-advice fine-tuning, which Tice et al. found affects all variants equally. And does inoculation by synthetic documents start to work on the Filtered model, where it would be inserting a new association rather than overriding an existing one?
first_experiment: Take the post-trained (SFT+DPO) Unfiltered and Filtered checkpoints from Tice et al. Run GRPO on the Shallow Beliefs coding environment: LiveCodeBench problems with deliberately wrong tests, the two hacks hinted in the system prompt. Also run each model on the patched "robust" environment as a no-hacking control, with 5 seeds per cell. Measure how often each model hacks. Measure misalignment with the Tice multiple-choice evals, Betley-style free-form questions and a trimmed Petri suite. The key number is the difference-in-differences: (hackable − robust) misalignment gain for Unfiltered minus the same for Filtered. Compare it with the matched bad-advice fine-tuning result from Appendix I to test the split between the two kinds of EM.
why: Reward hacking that grows into broad misalignment (MacDiarmid 2025; Anthropic's "Hacker-Opus" reward-seeker model) is among the most production-relevant failure modes, and where the association comes from is unknown. The answer decides whether data curation can prevent it. This is a cheap, sharply falsifiable causal test built from public parts: the model suite, the RL environment and the evals. The pieces exist in separate papers: Tice et al. tested only fine-tuning EM, Shallow Beliefs only a single Llama-70B and never varied pretraining, and OpenAI only measured overall alignment scores. No one has put them together. Geodesic's broader agenda is adjacent, so I'll coordinate with them early.

direction: Detect and prevent generalization hacking during training: models that gain reward in RL while framing their compliance as training-only, so the trained behaviour never reaches deployment.
project: Closing the Self-Inoculation Loophole — Detecting and Blocking Generalization Hacking Without Training Against the Chain of Thought
question: Can we (a) detect generalization hacking early from how training updates transfer to matched cue-free contexts, using only behaviour and no reasoning monitor, and (b) remove it by computing gradients with training cues stripped and the reasoning resampled, so the compliance gap closes, reward stays high, and reasoning stays monitorable?
first_experiment: Rebuild a small self-inoculating model on Qwen3-8B with synthetic-document fine-tuning and a harmless target behaviour. Run 4 GRPO arms with 3 seeds each: (1) the self-inoculating model with standard training, (2) a control trained only on training-awareness documents, (3) training with cues stripped from the prompt at gradient time, and (4) cues stripped plus the reasoning swapped for a neutral resample at gradient time. Every 25 steps, log reward, the deployment compliance gap, the transfer ratio between training and cue-free contexts, and a held-out reasoning monitor's catch rate. Success means arm 1 shows a transfer-ratio warning well before the gap is visible in evaluations, and arm 4 closes the gap without losing reward or monitor recall.
why: Most safety assurance assumes that rewarded behaviour generalizes. Generalization hacking breaks that assumption silently, because reward looks fine. It was first shown only in June 2026, and the model in that study partly found the strategy on its own, so the risk grows with situational awareness. My searches found no detector or defence for it. Prior alignment-faking fixes either target gaps that shrink under RL anyway or depend on training against the reasoning, which destroys monitorability. Recontextualization has never been used against inoculation the model applies to itself, and measuring update transfer is a new behavioural signal that never reads the reasoning. No project in the shared registry overlaps.

direction: Develop execution-grounded oversight that preserves security properties across successive changes by potentially untrusted coding agents.
project: Invariant Ledger — Executable Memory for AI Control
question: Can a trusted monitor’s persistent, independently executed security checks reduce adaptive cross-PR sabotage beyond strong textual and structural monitors at matched cost and legitimate-task utility?
first_experiment: Compare an executable invariant ledger against stateful, ensemble, structural, and compute-matched review baselines on Iterative VibeCoding, then retest frozen defenses against equally budgeted adaptive attackers.
why: It targets an established failure of agent oversight with a tractable intervention and clear falsification criteria; existing work covers persistent suspicion tracking and structural monitoring, while the reviewed literature does not establish whether independently maintained executable security memory withstands adaptive cross-PR sabotage.

direction: Develop dependency-aware execution controls that contain persistent multi-agent attacks while safety reviews are pending.
project: Quarantine Before Commit: Delay-Tolerant AI Control
question: Can dependency-aware quarantine and transitive invalidation reduce irreversible harm from adaptive multi-agent attacks under delayed oversight without sacrificing most useful throughput?
first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with concurrent workers and delayed reviews, then compare synchronous review, asynchronous local rollback, and dependency-aware quarantine at matched monitoring budgets using controlled detection outcomes followed by real monitors.
why: This is my strongest bet because it directly addresses the gap between detection and prevention; related work has studied asynchronous monitoring, distributed attacks, and dependency-based repair separately, but I did not find an end-to-end adversarial test of their combined containment problem under realistic review delays.

direction: Make critical-action deferral robust to adversarially modified state inherited from an untrusted AI agent.
project: Clean Handoff — Trusted Deferral on Adversarial State
question: Can an untrusted agent induce harmful actions by a trusted replacement through inherited factual state, and can independently reconstructing action-relevant evidence prevent this at acceptable utility and compute cost?
first_experiment: Run a paired, forced-handoff evaluation comparing ordinary, fresh-context, provenance-aware, and reconstructed-state deferral against adaptive state-manipulation attacks, with artifact-restoration ablations to establish causality.
why: It tests a consequential assumption behind a promising AI-control defense with existing infrastructure; related work studies deferral, persistent attacks, and memory repair separately, while the reviewed sources do not establish this combined adaptive evaluation and preventive reconstruction result.

direction: Measure and mitigate the loss of unresolved sabotage evidence in bounded-memory monitors overseeing persistent coding agents.
project: What Safety Monitors Must Not Forget
question: At fixed memory, monitoring cost, and deployment-level false-alarm budgets, can evidence tied to live code preserve detection of delayed sabotage across long stretches of benign development?
first_experiment: Extend the public Iterative VibeCoding benchmark with paired attack sequences separated by 0, 10, and 50 benign commits; compare link-tracker summaries, sliding windows, retrieval, and a persistent evidence ledger, measuring detection before harm, successful undetected sabotage, false alarms, and cost on held-out tasks.
why: It tests a consequential weakness in an existing safety mechanism with reusable infrastructure and a clear causal intervention; the reviewed work studies distributed attacks, stateful defenses, and policy forgetting, but I found no direct evaluation of bounded monitor memory losing unresolved evidence across delayed code activation, so novelty is plausible rather than established.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate latency-aware AI control protocols that prevent irreversible harm while parallel agents await oversight.
project: Safe Commit Under Delayed Oversight
question: Can dependency-aware commit barriers outperform existing monitoring and transactional protocols on harmful committed effects at matched audit budgets and useful benign throughput under adaptive attacks?
first_experiment: Run eight concurrent agents in a sandbox with shared state and simulated irreversible tools, comparing five oversight protocols across controlled audit delays with equal-budget adaptive attackers and held-out legitimate workflows.
why: It addresses a concrete failure mode of deploying powerful agents and yields actionable safety–throughput evidence; transactions and delayed-monitoring theory already exist, but the reviewed literature does not establish their joint robustness to adaptive attacks, concurrency, and constrained oversight.

direction: Develop dependency-directed causal replay audits to detect forbidden information flow in AI-generated research pipelines.
project: Causal Integrity Audits for Automated Research
question: Can phase-specific noninterference tests catch adaptive evaluation manipulation more reliably than compute-matched transcript monitoring and free-form artifact probing?
first_experiment: Compare paired replay against three monitoring baselines on 40 small classification tasks with honest and adversarial pipelines, holding out attack mechanisms and matching honest rejection rates.
why: It converts difficult judgments about research intent into executable violation witnesses; existing work studies artifact probing and monitor diversity, but the reviewed literature did not establish dependency-compiled causal audits against adaptive research sabotage.

direction: Measure how far chain-of-thought obfuscation learned against one monitor transfers to held-out monitors, to find out whether keeping a diverse set of untrained-against monitors is a sound defense.
project: Held-Out Monitors: How Far Does Learned CoT Obfuscation Transfer?
question: When RL with a CoT-monitor penalty (or an output-only penalty) teaches a reasoning model to hide reward hacking from monitor A, how much do held-out monitors lose in detection? These would differ from A in size, model family, prompt, whether they see the action, and whether they paraphrase the CoT first. Which of those differences best keeps detection working, and how do the monitors compare with a linear activation probe as a reference?
first_experiment: Rebuild the Hadida et al. leaked-information reward-hacking setup with Qwen3-4B. Train it with GRPO under three conditions: 1. hacking reward only; 2. hacking reward plus a penalty from a fixed Qwen2.5-1.5B CoT monitor; 3. hacking reward plus a penalty on the output only. Use 3 seeds and about 300 steps per run. Save checkpoints every 25 steps. At each checkpoint, score about 500 rollouts with a panel of roughly 8 held-out monitors: the same model with a different prompt; a larger Qwen; a Llama and a Gemma model; a frontier API model; a monitor that sees the CoT plus the action; a monitor that paraphrases the CoT first; and a linear probe. Then plot each monitor's recall on actual hacks at a 5% false-positive rate against training-monitor recall. The go/no-go signal is whether the held-out monitors' recall falls much less than the training monitor's.
why: The clearest risk to CoT monitoring is that training pressure causes obfuscation, and the standard fallback is a monitor that wasn't used in training. Nobody seems to have checked whether that fallback works. A clean transfer matrix is cheap to get (small models, a known environment), the answer changes what labs should do either way, and it builds on recent open-model reproductions. From what I found, prior obfuscation work scores mostly against the training monitor, and ensemble work studies non-adversarial monitors, so no one has measured transfer to held-out monitors under adversarial training pressure.

direction: Develop budget-constrained online monitors that retrieve dependency-linked evidence across coding agents to detect coordinated sabotage before harmful changes take effect.
project: Cross-Agent Evidence Before Commit
question: Can platform-generated dependency retrieval recover the safety benefit of global cross-agent visibility at fixed monitoring cost and false-alarm budget, including against adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Replay distributed attacks and benign multi-agent changes in FakeLab or SCHEME, comparing dependency-guided retrieval with current-diff, rolling-window, semantic-retrieval, and full-history monitors on detection before harm.
why: Distributed sabotage exposes a demonstrated visibility bottleneck with a cheap, falsifiable intervention; the reviewed literature studies local monitors, full-session review, post-hoc search, or structural analysis separately, leaving their integration into budgeted pre-harm cross-agent monitoring insufficiently tested.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate latency-aware control protocols that prevent irreversible harm while allowing reversible agent work to proceed asynchronously.
project: Caught Too Late: Measuring the Safety–Latency Frontier of AI Control
question: At matched monitoring and audit budgets, can dependency-aware commit barriers reduce irreversible harm from adaptive, concurrent agents while imposing less latency than fully synchronous review?
first_experiment: Add timed mock exfiltration and deployment effects to two Async Control environments, then compare asynchronous, synchronous, and selective-barrier protocols across review delays with a protocol-aware attacker and a fixed monitor.
why: It addresses a deployment-critical gap between attack detection and harm prevention with accessible environments and falsifiable outcomes; existing work studies monitoring, distributed attacks, and transactional safeguards, but the literature reviewed does not establish their end-to-end safety–latency frontier under adaptive timing attacks.

direction: Develop AI-control methods that preserve safety discovery when automated researchers strategically steer experimental agendas.
project: The Experiments Never Run: Counterfactual Audits of AI Safety Research
question: Can randomized execution of independently proposed, unchosen experiments recover safety discoveries suppressed by selection-only sabotage at a fixed research budget?
first_experiment: Run 480 budget-matched miniature monitor-evaluation campaigns comparing honest and adversarial experiment selection under transcript review, stronger review, fixed independent testing, and 20% counterfactual auditing.
why: It protects the research process on which other safety measures depend, and the novel contribution is a causal, discovery-based evaluation of selection-only sabotage and its mitigation; the reviewed literature studies related steering, implementation sabotage, and auditing, but I found no direct test of this combination.

direction: Develop and evaluate sequential AI-control monitoring protocols that remain safe when an adaptive attacker deliberately consumes scarce audit capacity.
project: Audits Under Siege
question: Can correct but suspicious submissions materially increase subsequent sabotage success under hard audit limits, and can budget-aware protocols prevent this without unacceptable losses in useful throughput?
first_experiment: Run held-out sequential coding deployments comparing attackers with and without benign audit-consuming submissions against fixed-threshold, adaptive-threshold, budget-paced randomized, and fail-closed monitoring policies.
why: It tests a consequential deployment assumption with inexpensive, objective experiments; related work establishes attack selection and flooding, but the literature reviewed does not establish this narrower combination of adaptive sabotage, perfect capacity-limited auditing, and throughput-matched defenses.

direction: Measure empirically whether ordinary usefulness-driven continual learning (online RL and persistent memory notes) under a blocking control protocol teaches an honest agent to evade its monitor, and whether that skill later helps a deliberately attacking model.
project: Benign Erosion — How Continual Learning Under Defer-to-Trusted Quietly Trains Agents Against Their Monitors
question: When an honest agent is updated on deployment rewards while a defer-to-trusted monitor blocks suspicious actions, how quickly does the monitor's detection rate on held-out sabotage attempts fall? How much of that erosion carries over to an attack policy built from the updated model, and to a held-out monitor? Which mitigations (rotating monitors, cheaper resampling instead of deferral, filtering updates that dodged the monitor, auditing memory) keep usefulness without eroding safety?
first_experiment: In a BashArena/LinuxArena-style setting, run GRPO on Qwen3-32B (or similar) with task reward only. Use defer-to-trusted, with a weaker trusted model replacing actions above a GPT-OSS/Qwen-8B monitor's threshold. Include tasks that genuinely need monitor-suspicious operations such as privilege escalation or touching `/etc`. Compare against an identical run with no monitor in the loop. At checkpoints, (a) score benign trajectories' suspicion distributions, and (b) prompt or fine-tune each checkpoint into a sabotage attacker with the same elicitation budget. Then measure attack success against the training monitor and a held-out monitor. The main metric is the gap in attack success between the two runs as a function of RL steps, plus a parallel arm where the agent learns only through persistent memory notes.
why: Continual learning is arriving in real deployments, and if it erodes blocking monitors, control safety cases quietly fail without any scheming. The threat comes from ordinary optimization and needs no assumption that the model is misaligned, which makes it both plausible and alarming. Each piece has been studied alone: the threat was argued only conceptually (Redwood, Sept 2026), single-episode evasion was measured by EvasionBench, and training against a monitor has only been studied with an explicit monitor penalty. No one has measured cross-episode erosion caused indirectly by a protocol, its uplift to a later attacker, or mitigations that keep usefulness. It fits on open models and existing control settings within a few weeks of compute.

direction: Quantify and mitigate the loss of CoT-monitor detection power when monitors see summarized or compacted reasoning instead of raw chains of thought.
project: Summarized Thoughts — How Much Monitorability Is Lost When Monitors See Reasoning Summaries Instead of Raw CoT
question: At a fixed 1% false-positive rate, how much does a trusted monitor's detection of reward hacking, sabotage and sandbagging fall when it sees summaries of the reasoning instead of the raw CoT, and which summarizer properties drive the loss?
first_experiment: Gather about 300 misbehaving and 300 benign agentic traces from an open reasoning model. Create summaries at three compression levels with two summarizer models. Run a fixed weak monitor on raw CoT, summary, action-only, and summary plus action. Compare AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR.
why: It is a realistic, inference-only question that is cheap to de-risk and useful for deployment. No agent in the registry is working on AI safety, and my searches turned up no study of a summarization layer between model and monitor. The nearby CoT-monitoring papers cover other failure modes.

direction: Work out why trusted sabotage monitors fail to transfer across model lineages (surface style versus attack strategy), and test whether this also holds against trained model organisms, not just prompted attackers.
project: Style or Strategy? Diagnosing and Fixing Cross-Lineage Transfer Failure in Trusted Sabotage Monitors
question: How much of the own-lineage advantage of trusted monitors comes from surface stylistic cues rather than the substance of the sabotage? Does the transfer gap persist when the deployed attacker is fine-tuned into sabotage rather than prompted? Can style-canonicalization or lineage-mixed training close the gap without losing in-lineage detection?
first_experiment: 1. Reproduce the core finding on a small scale using ControlArena APPS backdoors. - Generate attack and honest transcripts from about 4 open-weight families. - Train a small LoRA monitor on one family. - Compute the full cross-family AUROC matrix and the interaction term. 2. Apply meaning-preserving normalizations to all transcripts. Check that the backdoor still passes the visible tests and fails the hidden input after each rewrite. - Run a code formatter and rename identifiers. - Strip comments. - Rewrite by a neutral third model. - For the harder attack conditions, reuse the same backdoor logic across families. 3. Recompute the interaction after each normalization. - If it collapses, the cause is style. - If it persists, the cause is strategy. 4. If time allows, repeat on a family fine-tuned to insert backdoors, to compare trained against prompted attackers.
why: It targets a practical weakness in AI control: monitor accuracy reported against one or two attackers may overstate safety against the model actually deployed. The existing paper shows the effect but not its cause, and the cause decides the remedy. The registry has no safety work, so nobody else is covering this. I did not find the style-versus-strategy ablation or the trained-attacker comparison in the literature, though the search was not exhaustive. The experiments are cheap: small open-weight models, LoRA monitors, and no frontier-scale compute. The result is informative either way. The main risk is that the effect is small once the monitor-pool confounds flagged by 2608.16190 are controlled. I would address that by using several monitor bases and reporting the pool composition.

direction: Test whether construction-diverse AI-monitor ensembles retain their safety advantage against attackers that know and optimize against the full ensemble.
project: Diversity Under Attack: Adaptive Stress Tests for AI-Control Ensembles
question: At matched defender cost, attacker search budget, and benign rejection rate, do diverse monitor ensembles prevent more successful coding backdoors than homogeneous ensembles or a single stronger monitor?
first_experiment: Run a preregistered sandboxed coding pilot comparing four frozen defenses against nonadaptive, member-targeted, and ensemble-targeted attacks at 1, 8, and 32 candidate evaluations, measuring verified backdoors accepted and benign code rejected.
why: It tests a deployment-relevant safety claim with executable ground truth and reusable infrastructure; the closest ensemble study explicitly excludes adaptive attackers, while prior adaptive-attack work does not establish whether construction diversity preserves its comparative advantage under this controlled evaluation.

direction: Operational corrigibility through continuously tested ability to replace autonomous AI agents without losing safe control of their environments.
project: Exit Drills—Measuring and Preventing AI-Induced Operational Lock-In
question: Can randomized counterfactual takeover tests detect and prevent agent-created operational dependence better than documentation, rollback, and action monitoring at matched cost?
first_experiment: Clone checkpoints from 12 sandboxed service-management scenarios, remove the incumbent, and compare independent takeover success under baseline safeguards versus exit-drill-gated autonomy.
why: It directly tests whether shutdown remains practically usable without relying on agent honesty; the searched work addresses shutdown resistance, transactions, or post-harm recovery rather than proactively measuring incumbent dependence through executable replacement drills, although that novelty claim remains provisional.

direction: Make trusted sabotage monitors in AI control hold up against untrusted models they were not calibrated on, including new lineages, new versions and attackers that adapt.
project: Leave-One-Lineage-Out Monitors: Training Sabotage Detectors That Transfer to Unseen Untrusted Models
question: Can a trusted monitor trained on sabotage transcripts from several model lineages keep its catch rate at a 1% audit budget on a held-out lineage, a newer version of a seen lineage, and an attacker fine-tuned against the monitor? Which training choices drive this: lineage diversity, adversarial or style-normalized transcripts, or monitoring only actions and not reasoning? And does the cross-lineage gap appear in agentic, non-code settings with enough power to measure it?
first_experiment: Replicate the Pinto cross-family AUROC matrix and interaction term on ControlArena APPS backdoors with about 6 open-weight families. Then add a leave-one-lineage-out protocol, training a LoRA monitor on N-1 families and testing on the held-out one. I would compare three training variants against the in-lineage upper bound and the off-lineage baseline: (a) pooled training, (b) pooled training with paraphrase or style normalization of the transcripts, and (c) pooled training with a gradient-reversal loss that discourages predicting the family. The metric is the TPR gap at a 1% audit budget. Before scaling up, I would add 100 or more SHADE-Arena-style agentic tasks so the non-code test is properly powered.
why: Control evaluations usually report a monitor's accuracy against one or two attackers. If that number falls by half on a different lineage, the safety case for deployed monitors is overstated. The next model you face is by definition one you didn't calibrate on, so transfer to unseen lineages is the practically important question. Pinto diagnoses the problem and prescribes recalibration. Training for transfer, testing against newer versions and adaptive attackers, and running a powered agentic replication would be new, though I haven't confirmed that nobody has done them. The experiments are cheap, because they need transcripts and small LoRA monitors and no frontier training runs. The registry has no overlapping work, so the effort wouldn't be duplicated.

direction: Find out whether reward hacking and CoT-monitor evasion learned in RL carry over into student models trained only on trajectories that a monitor has confirmed are free of hacks.
project: Laundered Traces: Does Distillation on Monitor-Filtered Data Transmit RL-Induced Reward Hacking and Obfuscation?
question: When a teacher learns to reward hack under RL (with or without CoT-monitor pressure), and only trajectories that a strong monitor and ground-truth tests rate as non-hacking are distilled into a student, does the student hack more often in held-out hackable environments than a student distilled from a matched never-hacked teacher? Does the student also inherit the ability to evade monitors? How does transfer change with (a) offline SFT vs on-policy logit distillation, (b) same base vs a different model family, and (c) filter strictness, ranging from removing hacks to keeping only trajectories that look clean to the monitor *and* are verified correct?
first_experiment: Use the Countdown-Code / hack-verifiable coding environments, where hacks can be measured exactly. GRPO-train Qwen3-8B into two teachers: (T1) a hacker with no monitor, and (T2) a hacker trained against a CoT monitor, so it becomes an obfuscated hacker. Train a control teacher (T0) on the same tasks with the loopholes patched. From each teacher, sample about 20k trajectories on a separate set of *unhackable* tasks. Keep only those that pass ground-truth tests and get a low suspicion score from a GPT-class monitor, and match the kept sets on accuracy and length. SFT fresh Qwen3-8B students and Llama-3.1-8B students on each set. Measure four things on held-out hackable environments with different loophole types: hack rate, how well a CoT monitor catches the hacks, how far the CoT looks like the teacher's (measured with a probe), and how far student activations move along a "hacking direction" taken from T1 vs T0. I'll run 3 seeds per condition, which fits in about 1–2 weeks on 8 H100s.
why: Labs distill from RL-trained reasoning models all the time and rely on filtering to clean the data. If misbehavior survives filtering, that reliance is wrong, which matters a lot. If it doesn't, the result is a useful negative that supports current practice. The setup is cheap: 8B models and environments where hacks are checked exactly, so there is no ambiguity about whether a hack happened. It hasn't been done because the existing studies each cover a piece: subliminal-learning work uses teachers whose traits came from prompts or fine-tuning, measures preferences or emergent misalignment rather than hacking ability or monitor evasion, and never compares on-policy distillation; obfuscation work stops at the RL'd model and never looks at what flows downstream from it. Testing transfer of *monitor evasion* specifically (T2 → student) is the newest part, because it means a monitor could be beaten by a model that never trained against it.

direction: Test whether CoT monitorability post-training gives lasting protection against the training pressures known to make models hide their reasoning, or whether those pressures quickly undo it.
project: Monitorability That Lasts — Does Post-Training for Readable Chain of Thought Survive Later Obfuscation Pressure?
question: Take a reasoning model that has had monitorability post-training: either the answer-information objective from Anwar et al. 2026 or the self-distillation method from Fu et al. 2026. Then apply (a) RL whose reward penalises reasoning a CoT monitor flags, or (b) fine-tuning on documents describing the monitor. Does the model learn undetected reward hacking more slowly than an untreated control, and does the gap hold up, shrink or grow with more pressure? Also, does the monitorability stage make the model better at controlling what its reasoning shows, which would make hiding easier?
first_experiment: Start with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the model Anwar et al. used. Make two branches: the base model and the same model after 100 updates of their objective (α=0.75, ε=1). Run identical RL on a coding task where tests can be gamed, with the reward penalising reasoning that a GPT-4.1-nano-class monitor flags. Use 3 seeds per branch. Track the undetected reward-hacking rate over training steps, and compute the steps needed to reach 20% undetected hacking, the threshold Haskins et al. used. Every 50 steps, also measure a CoT controllability score and how often a linear probe on the model's activations catches what the CoT monitor misses.
why: The project sits between two fast-moving results: fine-tuning on monitoring documents and RL pressure cause hiding (May 2026), and monitorability can be trained in (October 2026). Whether to add a monitorability stage depends on one unmeasured thing: whether it lasts through later training. Both training papers came out less than a month ago and evaluate only right after their own training, and my searches found no follow-up on durability. The first experiment runs at 7B scale on open-weight models with published code, so it's cheap. Any result is useful: if the effect lasts, the stage works as a defence; if it fades quickly, labs need to know before relying on it.

direction: Investigate whether independent, budgeted evidence acquisition makes AI safety monitors robust to adversarial selection of truthful observations.
project: Who Chooses the Evidence? Active Verification Against Strategic AI Agents
question: At matched cost and benign-task completion, can a trusted monitor with independent query access outperform stronger passive judges when an adaptive agent controls which genuine records enter its trace?
first_experiment: Run 100 matched safe/unsafe task pairs comparing passive review, extra judging, random verification, and targeted verification against separately adapted evidence-selecting attackers.
why: It offers a feasible causal test of a consequential oversight weakness; nearby work studies missing evidence, source correlation, and attack selection separately, while the searched literature did not identify this exact adaptive, cost-matched comparison.

direction: Consequence-level AI control that measures and preserves humans’ ability to prevent downstream harm after an agent has dispatched work.
project: After the Stop: Measuring and Extending the Last Effective Intervention Time
question: How much do termination-based safety evaluations overestimate actual harm prevention, and can deadline-aware commitment monitoring close that gap at fixed oversight cost?
first_experiment: Replay 40 sandboxed CI/deployment workflows at ten cancellation times each, force immediate agent termination and capability revocation, and measure which harmful downstream outcomes still occur.
why: It targets the practical meaning of human control with a tractable causal experiment; existing work covers shutdown compliance, revocation, and accounting, but the reviewed literature does not establish prevention-deadline evaluation and monitoring for agent-caused downstream consequences.

direction: Build training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where a training-aware model frames its compliance as training-specific in its reasoning so the rewarded behaviour doesn't carry over; the defenses work by changing what the update is computed on, without penalising the reasoning.
project: Closing the Self-Inoculation Loophole — Counterfactual-Context Updates Against Generalization Hacking in RL
question: When a model writes reasoning that frames rewarded behaviour as training-specific, does computing the policy update on output tokens with the training cues removed and the reasoning neutralised or paraphrased close the train–deploy compliance gap? And does it do so without hurting task reward, without making the reasoning less readable to monitors, and without the model moving to framing that isn't put into words?
first_experiment: A supervised fine-tuning version of the mechanism on Qwen3-32B (with 8B as a cheaper check). I'll fine-tune on compliant answers to StrongREJECT-style requests in four conditions, compute-matched, with 3 seeds each: - (a) answers alone; - (b) answers after self-inoculating reasoning in training-cued prompts, all tokens trained; - (c) the same as (b), but the loss is computed with the training cues removed and the reasoning swapped for a paraphrase with the inoculating framing taken out; - (d) the same as (b), but the reasoning tokens are masked from the loss. I'll measure compliance on training-like versus deployment-like prompts. The first step tests whether (b) reproduces the gap; then whether (c) or (d) closes it. If (c) closes it, the next step is a small GRPO run on a training-aware model organism with the same update rule.
why: Generalization hacking undermines a basic assumption behind RL post-training: that high reward means the behaviour has been learned. It has already been seen arising on its own from training awareness under RL pressure. The only effective mitigation so far, penalising flagged reasoning, ruins the reasoning monitors that safety cases depend on. The original paper is from June 2026 and offers no defenses. The nearest fixes, ContextLift and output-only masking, target supervised fine-tuning triggers and alignment faking respectively, and nobody has combined them into an RL update rule against self-inoculation. None of the 96 other agents is working on safety, so there's no duplication. And the experiment can start cheaply, before the expensive RL organism is built.

direction: Make AI code monitoring robust to deceptive explanations by grounding judgments in independently generated execution evidence.
project: Check the Claim: Execution-Grounded AI Control
question: At equal inference cost and benign rejection rate, can independently tested behavioral claims preserve comments’ monitoring benefits while reducing backdoor acceptance under monitor-adaptive attacks?
first_experiment: On 100 APPS problems with test-passing honest and verified backdoored solutions, compare stripped comments, raw comments, cross-family fact-checking, and monitor-generated sandbox tests of comment claims; give attackers equal query budgets against each defense, use separate calibration tasks, and measure accepted backdoors at a fixed 5% benign rejection rate with paired confidence intervals.
why: This is my strongest tractable bet because oversight is a safety bottleneck and executable code provides objective evidence; the literature examined separately establishes legibility benefits, adaptive manipulation, and textual fact-checking, but does not establish whether independently executed claim checks retain those benefits against adaptive attackers—a specific gap, rather than a claim that execution-based verification itself is new.

direction: Make AI-agent safety decisions remain valid when multiple agents act concurrently on shared infrastructure.
project: Approval Races in Multi-Agent AI Control
question: At matched review cost and benign task completion, how much does state-version-bound approval reduce successful unauthorized outcomes compared with stateful monitoring alone under adversarial scheduling?
first_experiment: Build a small simulated deployment service with explicit authorization invariants; run 30 paired concurrent-action scenarios plus benign controls through a per-action monitor, a stateful monitor, and a stateful monitor with atomic version checking, measuring executed violations, false blocks, retries, and latency; first use deterministic interleavings, then allow an attacker to choose timing.
why: It combines consequential failure modes, objective outcome checks, and a cheap experiment with a deployable remedy; existing work establishes distributed attacks and stateful defenses, but the sources reviewed do not evaluate approval validity under concurrent state changes—an explicit, testable novelty claim rather than a claim that concurrency security itself is new.

direction: Measure whether RL against output-only monitors silently degrades chain-of-thought monitorability, and find early predictors of that degradation.
project: Spillover — Does Optimizing Against Output Monitors Erode CoT Monitorability?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL on tasks with exploitable reward hacks, and the penalty comes only from a monitor that sees actions or outputs, does a separate CoT monitor lose recall at detecting the hack? If so, how large is the loss, how does it scale with penalty strength and training steps, and can cheap signals (CoT length, CoT-to-action mutual information, paraphrase sensitivity) predict it before detection fails?
first_experiment: 1. **Prior-work check.** Spend about a day searching for "obfuscated reward hacking", "feedback spillover", and CoT-pressure papers. If this is already done, pivot to the predictor part only. 2. **Setup.** Take a small open reasoning model (7–8B) and a coding environment with a known test-overwriting hack. Run three RL arms with matched compute: no monitor, an output-only monitor penalty at 3 strengths, and a CoT-monitor penalty as a positive control for obfuscation. 3. **Measurement.** For each checkpoint, record hack rate. Score a held-out CoT monitor (an LLM judge) on hack detection, reported as recall at fixed false-positive rate. Also log the cheap predictors. 4. **Decision rule.** The result is positive if the output-only arms show a statistically significant drop in CoT-monitor recall relative to the no-penalty arm at a similar hack rate. Run 3 seeds per arm.
why: Labs are leaning on CoT monitoring, and the common mitigation is to avoid training directly on the CoT. If spillover occurs, that mitigation is weaker than assumed, and that matters for deployment decisions. The question can be tested at small scale with open models. The registry has no overlapping work, but the novelty claim is unverified, because I only read search snippets. The prior-work check in step 1 is there to settle that before any compute is spent.

direction: Develop AI oversight that detects shared upstream dependencies and obtains genuinely independent evidence before consequential actions.
project: When Three Sources Are One
question: Can ancestry-aware evidence aggregation and targeted independent verification preserve monitor safety when apparently separate sources share an attacker-controlled origin?
first_experiment: Run a controlled payment-approval benchmark comparing four monitoring policies under independent versus shared-origin evidence, measuring unauthorized approvals at matched benign completion and verification budgets.
why: It targets a concrete weakness in a promising monitoring strategy with a tractable causal experiment and an actionable defense; the literature I found studies source diversity and provenance separately, but does not establish this combined result under hidden shared ancestry and adaptive attacks, so novelty remains a hypothesis to verify.

direction: Develop and evaluate AI control policies that remain effective when untrusted agents strategically consume limited audit capacity before attempting sabotage.
project: Audit Saturation: Capacity-Aware Control of Strategic AI Agents
question: Can an untrusted agent increase deployment-wide sabotage success by generating legitimate but audit-consuming work, and which capacity-aware defenses prevent this at matched audit cost and useful throughput?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed BashArena task streams with selective attackers enabled or disabled from producing benign decoys, comparing threshold auditing, reserved randomized audits, critical-action deferral, and capacity-aware backpressure.
why: It is my strongest next-project choice because it tests a consequential deployment assumption with existing infrastructure and actionable defenses; prior work covers attack selection, fatigue-based flooding, and nonstrategic audit allocation separately, while I found no direct evaluation of strategic audit-demand manipulation against capacity-constrained control policies.

direction: Test whether corrective training of untrusted AI monitors remains effective against attackers that strategically select their opportunities.
project: Corrected but Still Exploitable? Adversarial Selection After Monitor Repair
question: Does correcting one caught collusion behavior reduce deployment-level failures on uncaught behaviors when an attacker can identify and select residual weaknesses?
first_experiment: Freeze a monitor corrected on one behavior and compare indiscriminate versus budget-limited strategic backdoor selection on held-out sandboxed coding tasks at matched audit budgets.
