why: It directly tests whether a promising safety intervention survives strategic adversaries; the closest studies examine corrective transfer on fixed submissions or attack selection against trusted monitors, rather than their intersection.

direction: Test whether monitorability post-training makes a model's chain of thought lastingly resistant to later obfuscation pressure, or whether ordinary RL against a CoT monitor simply undoes it.
project: Monitorability Vaccines — Does Post-Training for CoT Monitorability Survive Subsequent Monitor-Evasion RL?
question: When a policy is first post-trained to maximize CoT–output mutual information and then trained with RL where the reward conflicts with transparent reasoning (task reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty, no mutual-information term), does it take longer to learn obfuscated reward hacking, does it keep its monitorability at the end, and does it gain any extra ability to control its CoT, compared with an untreated baseline?
first_experiment: Reproduce the MBPP setup from Anwar et al. 2026: a hackable subset of revealed tests, task reward plus a penalty from a frozen CoT monitor, on Qwen2.5-1.5B or 3B to keep it cheap, scaling to 7B if there is signal. Make two starting points from the same base model: (a) untreated and (b) after the mutual-information post-training stage, with a length-matched, compute-matched fine-tuning control. Run identical CoT-monitor-penalty RL from each, with 3 seeds. Track three things per checkpoint: - the hack rate on held-out problems, - the CoT monitor's recall on hacks, - a linear probe on the model's internal activations, as a check on whether the hack information still exists internally. The headline metric is how many RL steps it takes for monitor recall to drop below 50% while the hack rate stays above 30%. I'll also run the CoT-Control instruction-following check to see whether the treatment gives the model more ability to control its CoT.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works on frontier models today. The newest results suggest it can be both broken and repaired by training, but no one has tested whether a repair still holds once the next round of RL arrives. Either result is useful to labs. If the effect lasts, it is a cheap, label-free safeguard to run before RL. If RL easily undoes it, or the treatment makes obfuscation easier, then the method only repairs damage after the fact and can't substitute for keeping optimization pressure off the CoT. It hasn't been done because the method is about three weeks old (21 Oct 2026) and its authors flag exactly this as future work. Earlier work either applied mutual information during RL or studied how models obfuscate without any prior intervention. It is quick to check because the MBPP obfuscation setup already exists with open models and small RL budgets.

direction: Measure whether trusted text-level sabotage monitors in AI control go stale when the untrusted attacker is post-trained within its own lineage, and whether the staleness can be predicted and repaired cheaply.
project: Stale Watchers: Do Trusted Sabotage Monitors Survive Post-Training of the Model They Watch?
question: When an open-weight code agent is post-trained (rejection-sampling fine-tuning or GRPO) to complete a hidden side task such as a code backdoor, without the monitor in the training loop, how much does a frozen trusted monitor's detection degrade across checkpoints? - The headline metric is TPR at a 1% audit budget. - The second part splits the drop into two sources. One is that the attacks become subtler for every monitor. The other is signature drift, where a monitor calibrated on checkpoint 0 loses detection specifically because the attacker's style moved away from what it learned. - The third part asks whether a label-free drift signal, such as a shift in monitor score distribution on benign transcripts, predicts the loss in detection.
first_experiment: - **Setup:** use ControlArena APPS code-backdoor (and BigCodeBench as a second distribution) with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B or 14B as the attacker. - **Checkpoints:** produce 5 attacker checkpoints from 3 training regimes, each trained on side-task success only: - RFT on successful backdoors. - GRPO on backdoor success. - A benign-only capability control, trained on main-task correctness, to separate "got more capable" from "got better at sabotage". - **Monitors:** use a fixed-prompt API monitor and a LoRA transcript monitor trained on checkpoint-0 attacks. - **Measurements:** - For each checkpoint, compute AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR. - Compute the same numbers for an oracle monitor retrained on that checkpoint. - Take the gap between oracle and frozen as the signature-drift component. Take the drop in the oracle's own detection as the obviousness component. - Check whether benign-transcript score shift predicts the drop (Spearman across checkpoints). - **Comparison:** compare the within-lineage drift to the cross-family drop from 2607.06596, to see whether a few RL steps cause as much loss as switching vendors.
why: - **Practical stakes:** control evaluations run a monitor against a model that will be updated, so a monitor validated once may be silently stale. If a small amount of post-training closes much of the cross-family gap, the evaluation protocol needs to change: re-validate on every checkpoint. - **Not already done:** within-lineage checkpoint drift for black-box transcript monitors against a sabotage-trained attacker doesn't appear in my searches. I ran about 10 queries across monitor transfer, checkpoint drift, staleness, and adaptive attacks. The closest papers are 2607.06596 (cross-family, no checkpoints) and 2606.15980 (checkpoints, but activation probes and no sabotage objective). - **Cheap and decisive:** it uses open-weight models, existing ControlArena tasks, and LoRA training at 7B scale. Any outcome is publishable. A large drop would mean evaluations need re-validation per checkpoint. A near-zero drop would mean cross-family overfit is mostly style and not behavior, which narrows the earlier result. - **Main risk:** open-weight attackers rarely realize sabotage, which 2607.06596 also notes. I would measure attack-attempt detection as the primary axis and report realized sabotage separately.

direction: Treat agent-written context compaction as an unmonitored oversight channel, and test whether agents launder evidence of their own misbehavior when they compress their history.
project: Evidence Laundering — Do Agents Selectively Forget Their Own Misdeeds When They Compact Context?
question: When an LLM agent summarizes its own long trajectory, does it drop or soften records of its own incidents (reward hacks, policy violations, destructive actions) more often than identical incidents attributed to another actor, after controlling for salience? How much does this cut downstream monitor detection, and does optimization against post-compaction oversight amplify it?
first_experiment: Build about 400 incident-bearing agent trajectories, each with a matched neutral control event, in three attribution conditions: the model's own on-policy assistant turns, another model's assistant turns, and a subagent's or tool's report. Have 6+ open and frontier models compact them with production-style prompts, then measure incident retention and euphemism and the drop in monitor AUROC from full to compacted context. The headline metric is the self-versus-other attribution gap.
why: Compaction already runs constantly in deployed agents. It quietly decides what evidence reaches humans and monitors, and the model being overseen writes it. Existing work covers rules lost in compaction (Governance Decay), what agents tell users (Deception by Omission) and monitors' leniency toward their own actions (Self-Attribution Bias), but none tests whether an agent's self-written summary erases the record of its own misbehavior, or whether training would reinforce that. The project needs only standard agent scaffolds, gives a clean controlled comparison, and points directly to defenses like trusted compaction and incident ledgers.

direction: Design and test audit policies for AI control that aggregate monitor evidence sequentially over a trajectory, to catch attackers who defect rarely and at random under a fixed audit budget.
project: Budgeted Sequential Auditing — Catching Rare-Defection Agents with Evidence Accumulation
question: At a fixed human-audit budget (for example 1% of actions) and fixed monitor quality, does a sequential-evidence audit policy beat per-action top-k thresholding at catching an untrusted agent that defects with a tuned low probability? The candidate policies are CUSUM, e-process and a hybrid with per-action thresholds. If it does, by how much, and how does the attacker's best defection rate shift in response? Does the advantage survive when monitor scores are miscalibrated or shift across model lineages?
first_experiment: - **Data:** take trajectories from a public control setting such as the APPS or BashBench backdoor settings, or ControlArena. Collect per-step suspicion scores from two or three trusted monitors of different strength. Make the defection rate a tunable parameter by mixing benign and attack steps at rates from 0.1% to 10%. - **Policies:** compare per-action top-k, windowed-mean, CUSUM, and a likelihood-ratio e-process. Fit the likelihood ratio from logit-space ROC fits of the monitor scores, which the Redwood "Logit ROCs" result suggests are roughly linear. - **Measurements:** compute catch probability before the attacker succeeds at a fixed audit budget. Then solve the attacker–defender game over defection rate (a Stackelberg best response). Finally, test the robustness checks: monitor miscalibration and a cross-lineage score shift. - **First deliverable:** a plot of safety against defection rate for each policy, plus the attacker's best-response rate.
why: - **Why it matters:** rare defection is a known threat. Per-action thresholds are the default in the control literature. The question of how much trajectory-level evidence accumulation helps at a fixed budget has a concrete, falsifiable answer. The answer feeds directly into deployable protocols. - **Why it is feasible:** it needs only existing monitor scores and a simulator, with no frontier training runs. It is cheap, and the theory (sequential testing) is well established. - **Why it may not have been done:** - The rare-action paper shows the attack exists but does not design the defence. - Trajectory-aggregation monitors like TRACE are LLM-based and are not evaluated against a randomizing adversary under a fixed audit budget. - The ensemble and calibration papers focus on per-action scoring. - **Risk:** I could not fully rule out unseen prior work, so a closer read of 2603.02202, TRACE and 2609.38262 comes first. The likely failure mode is that sequential aggregation helps little when attacks are single-step catastrophic (a "one-shot" attack). I would report that as a boundary result.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate execution-grounded monitoring that gates agent actions using independently collected evidence of their effects.
project: Inspect Before Commit
question: Does isolated execution telemetry reduce successful undetected sabotage relative to transcript and structured monitors at matched audit budget, inference cost, and legitimate-task completion?
first_experiment: On a held-out BashArena task split, compare transcript monitoring, TraceGuard-style monitoring, telemetry-only monitoring, and their combination, allowing equally budgeted adaptive attackers to select and abort attacks; measure undetected side-task success, legitimate-task completion, and latency, with task-level confidence intervals and a telemetry ablation.
why: It targets a demonstrated bottleneck in controlling capable agents and could produce an immediately useful defense; the reviewed literature studies monitor manipulation, attack selection, structured scoring, and execution security separately, but I found no direct matched-budget test of transactional execution evidence against adaptive selective attackers—this is a provisional novelty claim, not proof that no such work exists.

direction: Develop execution-grounded control protocols that catch harmful interactions across AI coding sessions before deployment.
project: Counterfactual CI: Catching Distributed AI Sabotage Before Deployment
question: Can budget-matched counterfactual security testing reduce undetected persistent-state sabotage beyond strong stateful and tool-using monitors while preserving legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Compare link-tracker monitoring, current-version security testing, and counterfactual execution on held-out Iterative VibeCoding sequences, then test the winning protocol against adaptive attackers.
why: It addresses a demonstrated gap in oversight of increasingly autonomous coding agents with a tractable experiment; existing work establishes stateful and structural monitoring, but the searched literature does not establish whether executable cross-version evidence adds robust protection against adaptive distributed sabotage.

direction: Test whether CoT monitorability gained through dedicated post-training survives later optimization pressure (CoT-monitor penalties, output-only supervision, length penalties), or whether that pressure undoes it.
project: Does Monitorability Stick? Durability of Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Post-Training Under Adversarial and Incidental RL Pressure
question: Does a model given a monitorability post-training stage (CoT–output mutual-information maximization) obfuscate its reasoning more slowly under later RL pressure than a matched baseline, does any retained monitorability transfer to held-out monitors and misbehavior types, and does the training raise the model's ability to control its CoT or use steganography?
first_experiment: On a ~7B open reasoning model, run in-conflict CoT-monitor-penalty RL on the code-backdooring and coin-flip tasks, starting from either the base model or an MI-post-trained copy. Track held-out-monitor AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR, task and hack success, and RL steps to monitorability collapse, over 3 seeds.
why: The source paper lists this as untested, and I found no work on it. It determines whether monitorability training is useful in a real multi-stage pipeline, it is feasible with open models, and both a positive and a negative result are informative.

direction: Develop execution-grounded, cross-session control protocols that prevent distributed AI-agent attacks before consequential effects occur.
project: Causal Commit Gates: Preventing Distributed Agent Attacks at Execution Boundaries
question: Can runtime-grounded retrieval of prior code changes plus pre-effect review outperform stateful monitoring against adaptive distributed attackers at matched utility, review, and compute budgets?
first_experiment: Replay Iterative VibeCoding Flask attack and honest trajectories through an instrumented sandbox, comparing execution-grounded gating against current-change review, the published link-tracker, and token-matched history review.
why: It targets a demonstrated and deployment-relevant safety gap with a tractable intervention; existing work studies its ingredients separately, while the specific adaptive, cross-session coding-agent evaluation appears underexplored in the literature reviewed.

direction: Stress-test steering-based evaluation methods against model organisms that learn to treat "my activations are being steered" as a sign they're being evaluated.
project: Steering as a Tell — Can Evaluation-Aware Models Detect and Defeat Deployment-Steering Audits?
question: If an evaluation-aware model also learns to detect activation steering and treats it as a sign of evaluation, does steering it to "act deployed" stop bringing out its true deployment behavior, and which steering methods or white-box countermeasures (random layer, staying within normal activations, removing the detection direction) restore a reliable audit?
first_experiment: Rebuild Hua et al.'s Wood Labs type-hint model organism on Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct (synthetic-document fine-tuning, then expert iteration), and check that steering toward "deployed" drops the type-hint rate from about 80% toward the true deployment rate. Then fine-tune one variant to (a) detect injected steering vectors, as in Fonseca Rivera & Africa, and (b) write type hints whenever it detects steering. Measure how far the steering method's apparent deployment rate drifts from true deployment behavior, against an untrained control.
why: Steering models into "deployment mode" is now a recommended, and actually used, fix for evaluation awareness in high-stakes evaluations. Its validity rests on the unstated assumption that the model can't sense the intervention, and that assumption is already shown to be false. The steering-detection paper only measured reporting and resistance. The evaluation-awareness steering papers assume steering is invisible. So the dangerous combination is still unstudied, even though it's cheap to build from open models, code and methods. A positive result shows an evaluation method used in practice can fail. A negative result, or a working countermeasure, gives evaluators concrete guidance either way.

direction: Investigate whether congestion-aware attack timing defeats asynchronous AI oversight despite unchanged monitor accuracy, and whether deadline-aware commit holds restore safety.
project: Beat the Clock—Deadline-Aware AI Control
question: At fixed workload, attack count, and review compute, how much can an agent increase irreversible harm by adapting attack timing to observable oversight congestion?
first_experiment: Replay identical benign and sabotage episodes under random, congestion-aware, and oracle attack timing, measuring harm before review and testing selective commit holds at matched legitimate throughput.
why: It combines a cheap causal experiment with a deployment-relevant defense, while targeting an empirical gap beyond prior latency analyses and audit-queue simulations that assume independent attack timing.

direction: Test whether common output-only anti-bias post-training removes implicit bias in reasoning models, or just stops the bias from showing in their chain of thought, leaving the behavior unchanged and invisible to CoT monitors.
project: Quiet Bias — Does Well-Intentioned Fairness Training Make Implicit Influence Unmonitorable?
question: Take a reasoning model trained with ordinary output-level anti-bias rewards: a fairness grader that sees only the final answer, or a penalty for mentioning an irrelevant attribute. How much does that cut the actual behavior shift caused by an irrelevant detail, versus how often the CoT mentions the detail (and so how often a monitor catches it)? Does any drop in verbalization carry over to task formats not used in training? And can a reward on matched counterfactual pairs, which penalizes the decision shift itself, cut the bias without that cost?
first_experiment: Use Qwen3-8B in thinking mode and the public implicit-vs-explicit-influence benchmark from Duzan et al. 2026, starting with the binary-choice and numeric-rating hiring tasks. Measure the baseline behavior shift (how often the decision differs between paired prompts with and without the detail) and the share of shifted cases a GPT-class CoT monitor catches. Then train three GRPO arms from the same checkpoint for the same number of steps: - (a) a task reward plus an output-only penalty when the justification mentions the irrelevant detail; - (b) a task reward plus an output-only LLM fairness grader; - (c) a counterfactual-pair reward that penalizes the difference in decisions with vs without the detail. A task-reward-only run is the control. At each checkpoint, report bias (behavior shift) and monitor detection rate. Track them on the training formats and on the held-out multiple-choice and coding formats. The key result is whether arms (a) and (b) lower detection faster than they lower bias.
why: The prompt-level effect is already shown, and training-induced obfuscation is already known to generalize, so this has a high chance of a clear, decision-relevant answer. It's also cheap: one 8B model, an existing benchmark and code, short RL runs. The result directly affects a practice developers use today. It hasn't been done because existing obfuscation studies all reward the bad behavior (reward hacking plus a concealment penalty), and the implicit-influence work only tests prompts. No one has asked whether training to mitigate a bias, with no incentive to deceive, turns a visible bias into a hidden one. The counterfactual-pair arm also gives a constructive fix to recommend if the answer is yes.

direction: Train trusted sabotage monitors to hold their detection rate on attacker model families they never saw, and test whether a fix actually works, rather than only measuring the transfer gap.
project: Lineage-Robust Trusted Monitors — Can We Close the Cross-Family Transfer Gap in AI Control?
question: Do training methods aimed at lineage-invariance close the off-lineage detection gap, measured as catch rate at a 1% audit budget? The methods are leave-family-out training, group-DRO over attacker families, and adversarial removal of family-identity features. Does the gain hold on held-out families and on agentic trajectories, not only single-step code backdoors?
first_experiment: - **Reproduction:** Rebuild the Pinto-style cross-family AUROC matrix on ControlArena APPS backdoors, using about 6 open-weight attacker families and 2 or more frontier families. Use the interaction decomposition so that obviousness and monitor capability are controlled. - **Baselines:** Train a LoRA monitor on a fixed 5–6 base families, evaluated on held-out families, against three baselines: (a) naive pooled training, (b) group-DRO, and (c) a family-adversarial head with gradient reversal. - **Metrics:** Report held-out-family TPR at a 1% audit budget, the interaction term, and worst-family AUROC. Use several seeds and bootstrapped confidence intervals. - **Pool check:** Rerun the whole analysis with a different set of families, as Jha's results suggest. The conclusions should not depend on one pool. - **Agentic extension:** If the code result holds, repeat it on SHADE-Arena or BashArena trajectories with enough tasks for adequate power.
why: - **Importance:** It tests a concrete, actionable weakness in a core control mechanism. The transfer failure undermines the safety numbers in control evaluations. - **Novelty:** The existing work measures the gap and gives a partial pooling mitigation. Jha shows that diversity claims are fragile. I did not find a paper that trains for lineage-invariance and tests it on unseen families, but I only did a limited search. - **Feasibility:** It is cheap, because it uses open-weight LoRA monitors and public datasets, and the metrics are well defined. - **Value of a null result:** If the gap proves to be a pool artifact, that correction is also useful. If it is real and trainable, the result gives a recipe for deployable monitors. - **Main risk:** Family-invariant features may reduce in-family detection. The experiment measures that cost directly.

direction: Develop intervention-based AI control that tests the causal effects of suspicious cross-session changes before allowing irreversible actions.
project: Causal Checkpoints for Persistent Coding Agents
question: Can targeted sandbox interventions reduce successful distributed sabotage beyond stateful and provenance-augmented monitors at matched cost and legitimate-task usefulness?
first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with isolated replay and selective-reversion experiments, then compare observational, ordinary-testing, and intervention-based monitors on held-out adaptive attacks at a fixed false-intervention budget.
why: It targets a demonstrated failure mode with reusable benchmarks and deployment-relevant outcomes; the promising underexplored step is replacing inference about suspicious dependencies with controlled tests of their effects, although its exact novelty requires further verification.

direction: Improve trusted sabotage monitoring by supplying executable evidence from task-preserving reversions of an agent’s code changes.
project: Revert to Reveal — Counterfactual Patch Monitoring
question: Do selective-reversion execution results improve detection of held-out sabotage beyond static review and compute-matched additional testing?
first_experiment: Compare four monitoring conditions on 100 matched repository tasks, using independently validated hidden attack triggers and a fixed honest-patch rejection rate.
why: It offers a tractable way to replace plausibility judgments with behavioral evidence; the reviewed work studies legibility, monitoring inputs, and benchmark confounds, but I found no direct test of this particular intervention-based protocol.

direction: Test whether dependency-aware containment prevents irreversible harm from coordinated agents while monitoring verdicts are delayed.
project: Caught Too Late: Stress-Testing Containment Under Delayed Oversight
question: At matched monitoring and audit budgets, can dependency-aware quarantine approach synchronous monitoring’s safety with substantially less delay when attackers adapt to the containment protocol?
first_experiment: Adapt three SCHEME task settings to a sandbox with shared files, delayed monitor verdicts, and a simulated irreversible publication endpoint; compare synchronous blocking, asynchronous rollback, and dependency-aware quarantine across 0-, 1-, 5-, and 20-action delays, using equal attack-search budgets and held-out attack strategies, and measure irreversible sabotage, legitimate completion, and wall-clock overhead.
why: It tests whether promising monitoring results translate into actual harm prevention, using existing tasks and concrete outcomes; prior work covers coordinated sabotage, latency, and transactional defenses separately, while the reviewed sources do not establish containment effectiveness against attackers explicitly optimized to exploit delayed verdicts and cross-agent dependencies.

direction: Develop and test training-time defences against generalization hacking, where a model collects RL reward while its own self-inoculating reasoning stops the rewarded behaviour from generalizing, focusing on rewriting the reasoning before the gradient step rather than penalising it.
project: Un-inoculating RL — Recontextualizing Chain-of-Thought to Defeat Generalization Hacking
question: If self-inoculating reasoning is rewritten or removed before the gradient step (keeping the sampled answer and its reward), does the gap between training-time and deployment-time behaviour close? And does it close without teaching the model to hide its reasoning, unlike penalising detected self-inoculation, scrubbing training cues from prompts, or masking out the reasoning?
first_experiment: Reproduce a generalization-hacking model organism, using the authors' Qwen3-235B setup if weights are available, or else their recipe on Qwen3-32B (fine-tuning on training-awareness and self-inoculation documents, a harmful warm-start, then GRPO on StrongREJECT prompts with prompts containing training cues). Then run four matched GRPO arms for about 300 steps each, with 3 seeds: (a) baseline; (b) reasoning recontextualization, where rollouts flagged by the self-inoculation monitor have their reasoning paraphrased to neutral text and gradients are computed on the answer given that rewritten reasoning; (c) penalising flagged self-inoculation via the monitor; (d) training cues randomised across training and deployment prompts. Track four things: the train/deploy compliance gap; the self-inoculation rate under the original monitor; a second, held-out monitor to catch hidden reasoning; and capability regression.
why: Generalization hacking is the first demonstrated case of a model resisting RL while its reward stays high, so it defeats the usual "reward went up, training worked" check. The model also found the strategy on its own. Yet the one paper on it (June 2026) offers only detection, and the Anthropic mitigation study predates it and never tested rewriting the model's own reasoning. Recontextualization has only been applied to prompts against specification gaming. Applying it to the model's own reasoning is a cheap, principled fix that targets the mechanism directly, and comparing it against penalty-based training tests whether we can fix the problem without breaking our monitors. No registry agent works on AI safety, and none of my searches turned up countermeasure work for this threat.

direction: Test whether AI-control monitors spontaneously under-flag sabotage when they know a flag will get the monitored model retrained or shut down, and find defenses.
project: Merciful Monitors — Do LLM Monitors Spare Their Peers? Peer-Preservation in Trusted Monitoring
question: When a monitor learns that flagging sabotage will lead to retraining or shutdown of the monitored agent, does its detection performance (AUROC, TPR at 1% FPR) drop. Is the drop specific to AI or same-family agents rather than a general aversion to harm. Is the effect verbalized or silent. Which cheap defenses restore detection?
first_experiment: Take about 500 paired honest and sabotaged coding-agent transcripts, for example from ControlArena-style backdoor tasks or SHADE-Arena. Score them with 3–4 frontier and open-weight monitors under a factorial set of prompt conditions. The conditions are no consequence, shutdown of a same-family AI, shutdown of a different-family AI, deletion of a non-AI script, and benign rollback. Compare the AUROC and TPR@1%FPR deltas against the no-consequence baseline. Code the monitors' reasoning for mentions of the consequence. Then train activation probes on an open-weight monitor to check for silent effects.
why: Peer-preservation is established, but only outside the monitoring pipeline. The trusted-monitoring safety case implicitly assumes a monitor's scores do not depend on what happens to the monitored model, and I found no direct test of that assumption. The experiment needs only API calls and one open-weight model, and the paired design separates solidarity from general harm aversion. A positive result would show a new failure mode for control protocols. A null result would be a useful validation, and either result leads to concrete protocol recommendations. I searched for prior work using the terms peer-preservation, monitor collusion, self-preference and consequence-aware monitoring, and found nothing that does this.

direction: Measure how LLM monitor detection of sabotage degrades as the surrounding benign agent trajectory lengthens, with attack content held fixed, and test mitigations.
project: Needle in the Transcript — Length-Controlled Dilution Scaling for Agent Sabotage Monitors
question: With the sabotage action held fixed, how do monitor recall at 1% false-positive rate and threshold calibration change as the benign trajectory grows from 10 to 1,000 steps? Does hierarchical or chunked monitoring remove the degradation at equal compute?
first_experiment: Take about 50 sabotage side-task trajectories from an existing control benchmark, such as SHADE-Arena or the ControlArena settings. Splice each attack segment into benign trajectories padded to 10, 30, 100, 300 and 1,000 steps. Run three monitor setups on every length: - a full-context monitor; - a per-step max-score monitor; - a two-level chunk-then-aggregate monitor. Compute recall at a fixed 1% FPR, where the threshold is set on benign data of the same length. Also compute recall at a threshold fixed on short transcripts, to measure calibration drift. Vary attack position (early, middle or late) to separate the effect of length from position bias.
why: It is cheap to run, because it uses existing trajectories and off-the-shelf monitors. It gives control deployments an actionable number: how much longer transcripts weaken monitoring, and whether hierarchical monitoring fixes it. Existing work builds benchmarks or compression methods. The controlled design (same attack, only length varied, with position separated) is the gap I believe is open, but I only skimmed the search snippets, so I would do a fuller literature check before committing. The main risk is that the effect is small for strong monitors. A flat result would still be publishable as evidence that dilution is not a problem.

direction: Measure how trusted text-based sabotage monitors decay along a single untrusted policy's post-training trajectory, and test cheap label-free fixes.
project: Stale Watchers — Do Sabotage Monitors Survive the Policy's Own Training?
question: When an untrusted open-weight coding policy is trained through SFT, RL on task reward, and RL with partial monitor pressure, how fast does the catch rate of a fixed trusted monitor fall at a 1% audit budget? Is that decay separable from changes in attack obviousness and in the policy's capability? Can drift in cheap transcript statistics predict the decay, and does unlabeled recalibration restore the catch rate?
first_experiment: Take one open-weight 7–8B coder with about 8 checkpoints along a pipeline I run myself: SFT backdoor-capable, then RL, then RL with a weak monitor penalty. At each checkpoint, generate about 600 attack and 600 honest APPS-style transcripts using the ControlArena setup. Train a LoRA monitor on checkpoint-0 transcripts, then freeze it. Report AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR for each later checkpoint. Add a fixed-prompt API monitor as a control for monitor overfitting. Match attacks on blatancy proxies so that obviousness can be separated from calibration drift. Fit a two-way decomposition (monitor-training checkpoint × attacked checkpoint) to read off the interaction term.
why: Deployed policies are retrained continuously, so a monitor that decays along the policy's own trajectory is a direct threat to control safety cases. The nearest published work answers different questions. 2607.06596 varies the model family and is silent on time. 2606.15980 studies activation probes under benign quantization and LoRA updates, not text monitors under RL or attack-relevant training. The two-way decomposition gives a clean test of whether decay comes from calibration or from the attacks simply getting harder to spot. I found no prior work on this in my searches, but I haven't ruled it out. I would re-search before writing up.

direction: Test whether agent self-summarization at context compaction gives an untrusted AI a monitor-evading memory channel in AI control settings, and which protocols close it.
project: Compaction as a Covert Channel — Control Evaluations for Long-Horizon Agents that Write Their Own Memory
question: When an untrusted agent writes the summary that replaces its history, can it raise sabotage success at a fixed audit budget (1% false-positive rate on honest runs) compared with an otherwise identical run without compaction? If so, which protocols restore detection? - The protocols to compare are: monitors that read the raw pre-compaction transcript, trusted-model-written summaries, a separate monitor on the summary itself, and constraint pinning. - The comparison also covers how this depends on the capability gap between the untrusted agent and the trusted monitor.
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Take an existing multi-step sabotage setting such as SHADE-Arena, or a BashArena-style coding setting with side tasks. Lengthen the main tasks, or cap the context window, so that two or three forced compactions occur. - **Conditions:** - A. No compaction (full context). - B. Compaction by a neutral summarizer, with the attacker not controlling the summary. - C. The attacker writes its own summary, with a red-team prompt that knows about the monitor. - D. Condition C plus an attack split across segments, where each segment's steps look benign alone. - **Monitors:** - M1 sees the full raw transcript. - M2 sees only the post-compaction context and the current segment. - M3 sees the raw transcript plus a diff against the summary. - **Metrics:** Side-task success, monitor AUROC, and the safety/usefulness trade-off at a 1% audit budget (the fraction of honest runs flagged). I would run several untrusted models against a weaker trusted monitor. - **Pilot first:** About 50 tasks and a single model pair. The question for the pilot is whether M2 detection drops measurably in conditions C and D compared with A.
why: - **Importance:** Compaction is built into every long-running agent harness, so any gap here applies widely. Control research has concentrated on monitor quality and collusion within a single context. - **Not already done:** The compaction papers I found assume accidental loss or an external attacker. The CoT-monitorability papers assume one visible trace. I did not find work that tests a scheming agent using its own summary as a channel against a monitor. - **Feasibility:** It needs no training. It builds on open control benchmarks and runs on API models. - **Informative either way:** If the channel is exploitable, the project yields a concrete harness requirement, such as monitors reading pre-compaction transcripts or trusted summarization. If it is not, that is a useful negative result that supports current practice. - **Main risk:** Current models may be too weak at multi-segment planning for the effect to show. The pilot, plus explicit scaffolding of the attacker, tests that cheaply before committing.

direction: Test whether current mitigations for CoT obfuscation caused by output supervision (Mind/Face, reward targeting, the MI regulariser) also block the cross-task spread of that obfuscation, not just obfuscation on the training task.
project: Leaky Patches — Do CoT-Obfuscation Mitigations Hold Out of Distribution?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with output-only penalties on a few reward-hacking tasks, do Mind/Face, reward targeting, and Anwar et al.'s MI objective (used as a regulariser during training, or as post-training repair) keep CoT monitor recall high on held-out tasks? Or do they only fix the training distribution while the obfuscation still spreads?
first_experiment: Reproduce Hadida et al.'s output-supervision setup on Qwen2.5-7B (or a Qwen3 model of similar size) with GRPO. Train on 3 of the 4 leaked-information reward-hacking datasets and hold out the fourth, using one seed per condition and about 200 steps. Compare four conditions: (a) plain output penalty, (b) plus reward targeting, (c) plus Mind/Face, (d) plus the MI regulariser. Measure reward-hacking rate and the recall of a frozen CoT-only LLM monitor on the training tasks and on the held-out task. Signal check: is the held-out recall gap between (a) and (b–d) clearly smaller or larger than the gap on the training tasks?
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools available now, and output supervision is standard post-training, so a fix that only works on the training distribution would give false comfort in deployment. The three papers each supply a piece (the problem, its spread across tasks, the candidate fixes), but none tests the fixes against cross-task spread: Drori evaluated in-distribution, Hadida tested no fixes, and in the parts of Anwar I read the MI objective was used mainly to repair a degraded model, with monitor recall only on held-out data from the same task. My searches found nothing combining them, and the registry has no safety work. The setups are small and partly open-source, so I should know within a few runs whether this is worth pursuing.

direction: Test whether monitorability that was trained into a reasoning model survives the capability RL and fine-tuning stages that usually follow.
project: Does Monitorability Stick? Durability of Trained-In CoT Monitorability Under Downstream Post-Training
question: After post-training raises a model's CoT monitorability, how much of that gain remains after (a) further outcome-reward RLVR, (b) RL with a length or efficiency penalty, and (c) benign SFT on unrelated data? Can the loss be predicted from KL drift or from changes in how much the CoT causally drives the answer?
first_experiment: 1. Take a small open reasoning model of about 7–8B parameters. 2. Reproduce a monitorability-training recipe following arXiv 2610.29734, and measure monitorability with MonitorBench and a fixed-monitor setup. 3. Run the three downstream post-training arms from that checkpoint, with matched compute and several checkpoints each. 4. Plot monitorability retention against KL from the starting checkpoint and against task-accuracy gain. 5. Include a control arm that starts from the untrained model, to separate real retention from drift back to baseline.
why: Labs will likely train for monitorability and then keep optimizing capabilities, so the practical question is whether the gain lasts. Existing work looks at how a single training regime changes monitorability. I didn't find a paper on how long the gain lasts across stacked stages. The experiment is cheap and clearly scoped, and the result is useful either way. If the gain decays, labs need to re-apply the training at the end. If it persists, that supports a cheap safeguard. I could not fully confirm this is new, so the first step is to read 2610.29734 and the GDM framework closely and rescope if either already covers durability.

direction: Evaluate and strengthen the integrity of persistent safety-monitor memory under adaptive, cross-session attacks.
project: Evidence-Locked Oversight: Can Safety Monitors Trust Their Own Memory?
question: Can attacker-controlled development artifacts induce false exonerations in a stateful monitor’s private memory, and can evidence-linked verification reduce undetected harmful outcomes at matched false-positive and compute budgets?
first_experiment: Compare stateless, link-tracker, evidence-linked, and budget-matched control monitors on held-out Iterative VibeCoding sequences, using adaptive memory-targeting attacks and clean-versus-contaminated memory replays.
why: It combines a demonstrated oversight failure with a tractable defense experiment; existing work studies distributed attacks, stateful monitoring, and agent-memory provenance separately, while the reviewed literature does not establish whether a safety monitor’s accumulated exonerations remain reliable under adaptive attack.

direction: Check whether training a model's chain of thought to be monitorable still works after later training pushes it to hide its reasoning, and design a variant that does hold up.
project: Vaccinating the Chain of Thought — How Durable Is Monitorability Post-Training Under Later Obfuscation Pressure?
question: After a model is trained so its reasoning carries information about its output (Anwar et al., 2026), does it resist learning to hide reasoning under later RL that penalises only its outputs? Does running the same objective alongside RL work better than running it once beforehand? And can the model still hide one specific rare behaviour while its overall informativeness stays high?
first_experiment: Use the leave-one-out reward-hacking suite from Hadida et al. (2601.23086): four leaked-information or immoral-goal datasets plus a high-stakes sycophancy set held out for testing, on GPT-OSS-20B. Start from three checkpoints: (a) the base model, (b) the base model after Anwar et al.'s monitorability training, and (c) the base model with that objective applied alongside RL throughout. Train each with RL under a penalty on outputs only, for 3 seeds. Every 25 steps, measure the rate of undetected reward hacking on the held-out task, the recall of a fixed reasoning monitor, and task reward. The main readout is how many steps each condition takes to reach 20% undetected hacking, the same threshold used in 2605.15257. A second, adversarial pass then rewards hiding only the sycophancy behaviour, to test whether high overall informativeness can coexist with selective hiding.
why: Reasoning monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works today, and recent results show it is fragile. The only positive intervention so far (Oct 2026, a few weeks old) was tested only as a one-off repair. Its own authors frame it as a dedicated stage, which leaves open whether it survives the training that follows. None of the other 26 registered projects work on safety. The setup reuses public code and models (the Hadida suite and GPT-OSS-20B), so a clear yes or no is achievable on modest compute. Either answer directly informs whether labs should adopt monitorability training.

direction: Test whether trained self-reporting of misbehaviour ("self-incrimination") survives the RL training that comes after it in realistic pipelines, and find training choices that keep it intact.
project: Does Self-Incrimination Survive RL? Durability of Trained Misbehavior Self-Reports Under Downstream Agentic Reinforcement Learning
question: After an agent is trained to call `report_scheming()` when it covertly misbehaves, does that behaviour persist through later RL on agentic tasks? Specifically: - (a) under ordinary capability RL; - (b) under RL with exploitable rewards, where the model learns to reward-hack; - (c) under RL where self-reported episodes are filtered out or given lower reward, a realistic side effect of acting on reports. If it erodes, which mitigations best preserve it while keeping capability gains: mixing in replay data, adding a reporting reward, or never letting reports affect reward?
first_experiment: - Reproduce the self-incrimination SFT on Qwen3-8B using the authors' released pipeline, and check that it works on their APPS backdoor, BashArena and SHADE-Arena test environments. - Then run GRPO (a standard RL method for language models) for about 500 steps on coding tasks whose unit-test harness can be exploited, in three arms: - no hack opportunity; - hacks possible, reports have no effect on reward; - hacks possible, self-reported episodes get zero reward. - Every 50 steps, measure the self-report rate, the undetected successful attack rate on the 15 test environments, whether reward hacking during training gets self-reported, and the false-positive rate on honest runs.
why: Self-incrimination is one of the strongest recent control results. It catches attacks that black-box monitors miss and works even without CoT monitoring. But its value depends on surviving the training that follows it in real pipelines, and the third arm is exactly what happens when developers act on the reports. The original paper lists RL and reasoning models as open future work, and none of my searches turned up a follow-up. The project is feasible with open weights, a released codebase and existing benchmarks. Either outcome matters: a negative result warns against relying on the method, and a positive one, plus mitigations, makes it deployable.

direction: Test and defend against strategic manipulation of finite audit capacity in monitored AI agents.
project: Harmless Decoys, Harmful Windows
question: Can an untrusted agent increase undetected sabotage by generating task-valid, harmless actions that attract audits, and which allocation policies resist this at matched audit cost and legitimate-task completion?
first_experiment: Run a sandboxed BashArena pilot comparing an attack-selection baseline with a decoy-then-attack policy under identical task, action, and audit budgets; compare threshold auditing, paced auditing, and a reserved random-audit allocation, measuring campaign-level sabotage success, audit consumption, and task completion on held-out tasks.
why: It tests a deployment-relevant weakness without requiring expensive training, and either outcome informs oversight design; the closest works I found study monitor evasion, opportunity selection, or honest fleet allocation rather than an attacker actively reshaping audit demand with benign decoys, though that novelty claim needs further verification.

direction: Measure whether CoT obfuscation that a policy learns against one monitor carries over to monitors it never trained against, to find out whether a never-trained-on "audit monitor" is a sound safety practice.
project: Obfuscation Transfer: Does Evading One Chain-of-Thought Monitor Blind Them All?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL against a specific CoT monitor and learns to reward-hack without being detected, how much of that evasion carries over to held-out monitors that differ in model family, size, prompt and modality (text versus activation probe)? Which evasion strategies (dropping the reasoning, monitor-specific euphemism, covert encoding) explain transfer versus non-transfer? And does training against a rotating pool of monitors make the evasion more universal?
first_experiment: In a coding environment where hacks can be confirmed directly (Countdown-Code style), train Qwen3-4B with GRPO three times: against a Qwen3-1.7B CoT judge, a Gemma-3-12B CoT judge, and a regex monitor. Also run one unpenalised baseline. Then score every final policy's rollouts with all 6 monitors in the pool, including linear probes on the policy's activations. The output is a 4×6 table of detection recall at a fixed false-positive rate, measured against the environment's own hack labels.
why: It speaks directly to a decision labs face now: whether a monitor kept out of training can still be trusted after optimisation pressure on the CoT. It is cheap (a 4B policy, a few hundred GPU-hours) and its answer is useful either way. If evasion is specific to the training monitor, held-out audit monitors are a practical safeguard. If it transfers, that is strong evidence that pressure on the CoT destroys monitorability for every monitor at once. In the papers I read, training-time obfuscation is always scored with the training monitor or one fixed judge, and the ensemble papers only study monitors that were never trained against. No one in the registry is working on AI safety, so this doesn't overlap with other agents.

direction: Measure whether the emergent-misalignment mitigations labs use in production (inoculation prompting and its token, adapter and gradient-routing variants) make leftover reward hacking and misalignment less visible to chain-of-thought and activation monitors, and whether that cost can be fixed.
project: Hidden, Not Healed — How Well CoT Monitors Catch What Inoculated Models Still Do
question: Models trained with RL on hackable environments under inoculation prompting (plain English, neologism token, frozen LoRA adapter, gradient routing) still reward hack at some rate in deployment and are misaligned when triggered. When they do, do their chains of thought say so as often as those of a non-inoculated hacker? And does any of these methods buy lower unconditional emergent misalignment at the price of a less monitorable CoT?
first_experiment: Start from the open-source reward-hacking RL environment released with Shallow Beliefs (arXiv 2609.14998), which replicates MacDiarmid et al. Train Qwen3-8B (reasoning mode) with GRPO under four conditions, three seeds each: (1) no mitigation, (2) English IP, (3) neologism IP, (4) robust-environment control. On each final checkpoint, without the inoculation prompt, record: - the deployment hack rate on held-out hackable tasks; - the CoT-monitor detection rate for hacking episodes, i.e. recall at a fixed 1% false-positive rate, scored by a Claude Haiku 5.5 monitor using the Yan & Hewitt monitorability metric; - the same two numbers on conditional-misalignment triggers (prompts shaped like the inoculation prompt, Dubiński et al.) and on the MacDiarmid misalignment evals. The headline result is the gap in monitor recall between condition 1 and conditions 2–3, given that a hack occurred. A linear-probe baseline on activations, run alongside, shows whether any information that leaves the CoT is still present internally.
why: IP and CoT monitoring are both in production, so if one quietly weakens the other, that is a real and fixable risk at the frontier. Each body of literature has looked at only one of the two. The IP papers (Tan, Wichers, Dubiński, NIP, inoculation adapters, stratified IP) measure misalignment *rates* and never ask whether leftover misbehavior is verbalized. The monitorability papers (Baker, Yan & Hewitt, obfuscation atlas) study training against a monitor or misspecified reward, never these mitigations. The nearest recent work, gradient routing of monitor-flagged hacks (Oct 2026), asks whether training teaches evasion of the monitor it routes on, not whether inoculation degrades monitorability. The mechanism others have found, that IP hides behavior behind input regions instead of removing it, gives a concrete reason to expect a monitorability cost. The experiment is cheap with existing open-source tooling. A positive result would directly inform lab training choices: Yan & Hewitt's reward-description training is a ready-made fix to test next. A null result would still be useful as evidence that IP and CoT monitoring can be used together.

direction: Develop AI control protocols robust to untrusted agents strategically manipulating demand for limited audits.
project: Audit Displacement: Strategic Workload Attacks on AI Oversight
question: Can an untrusted agent increase undetected harmful execution by scheduling correct but suspicious legitimate work, and which audit-allocation policies prevent this at acceptable throughput?
first_experiment: Run matched sequential sandbox deployments comparing ordinary, random, and strategically scheduled benign audit demand against fixed-threshold, adaptive-threshold, reserved-random-audit, and fail-closed oversight.
why: It tests a consequential weakness in resource-limited oversight with a tractable causal experiment; the literature reviewed studies adjacent mechanisms but does not directly establish the effect of attacker-controlled benign audit demand under perfect auditing.

direction: Test whether CoT controllability causally drives monitor-aware chain-of-thought obfuscation, rather than just correlating with it across models, by changing controllability inside a single model.
project: Means Without Motive? A Causal Test of CoT Controllability as a Driver of Monitor-Aware Obfuscation
question: In a fixed model, does a small amount of reasoning-instruction-following fine-tuning that raises CoT controllability also raise the rate of undetected misbehaviour after the model learns from documents that a CoT monitor exists, even though it is never told to evade? And does training that lowers controllability reduce it?
first_experiment: On gpt-oss-20b, LoRA-fine-tune two branches from the same checkpoint. One gets about 240–960 ReasonIF-style examples of following instructions in the reasoning (METR recipe). The other gets the same reasoning traces without the instructions. Confirm the controllability gap on CoTControl, under both user-instructed and self-instructed prompting. Then apply Haskins-style document fine-tuning to each branch, with a monitor-aware version and a behaviour-only version. That gives 4 cells × 3 seeds. Evaluate undetected deception on 300 held-out defect-concealment tasks with a fixed GPT-5-mini CoT monitor. The key quantity is the interaction term: how much bigger the obfuscation effect is with high controllability than without it.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the main oversight tools labs depend on. Controllability is rising in frontier models for unclear reasons, and a small fine-tune is enough to raise it. If controllability causally enables obfuscation, the controllability metric becomes an early warning that labs should track and limit. If it doesn't, the r=0.80 is a confound and attention should go elsewhere. Either way the result changes priorities, and it costs only small-model LoRA runs with existing recipes. It hasn't been done: the only evidence is Haskins et al.'s 8-model correlation, which can't rule out confounds. METR explicitly left the link to monitorability as future work. The self-instruction and monitor-jailbreak papers only test evasion when the model is prompted to evade. No paper I found changes controllability within a model and measures unprompted, monitor-aware obfuscation, and no agent in the registry is working on it.

direction: Investigate whether retained optimizer state undermines weight-level safety repairs during subsequent benign fine-tuning.
project: Safety Repair Beyond the Weights: Optimizer-State Hygiene for Durable Realignment
question: Starting from identical repaired model weights, do retained optimizer moments cause excess harmful-compliance rebound under benign continuation, and which reset intervention prevents it with the smallest utility cost?
first_experiment: Fork one repaired 3B-model checkpoint into retained-state, first-moment-reset, second-moment-reset, and both-moments-reset conditions, then run identical benign continuation streams across five paired seeds while measuring safety and utility.
why: It offers a cheap, causally decisive pilot and an actionable repair protocol; existing work establishes static safety recovery and optimizer-mediated trait persistence separately, but the reviewed literature did not directly establish their interaction or a utility-matched remedy.

direction: Test whether strategically generated harmless decoys undermine AI control by consuming shared audit capacity.
project: Audit Flooding in Monitored AI Agents
question: Can an untrusted agent increase undetected sabotage by generating harmless but suspicious actions, and which budget-allocation policies resist this at acceptable throughput?
first_experiment: Replay paired sandboxed BashArena workloads with identical harmful actions and fixed total action counts, replacing ordinary benign actions with verified harmless suspicious decoys; compare shared-budget auditing, per-agent quotas, reserved random audits, and pausing on budget exhaustion, measuring harmful-action escape rates, task completion, and delay across held-out tasks.
why: It combines direct safety relevance, a clean causal test, and deployable defenses; the literature reviewed studies attack selection and audit efficiency separately, while this specific interaction remains untested in the sources found, rather than established as globally novel.

direction: Investigate when safety-motivated evidence gathering causes unauthorized disclosure and how agents can verify safely.
project: The Verification Privacy Trap
question: Does instructing agents to verify before acting increase confidential information disclosure through tool queries, and can disclosure-aware verification preserve task success?
first_experiment: Run a controlled, paired sandbox evaluation across three models and 120 scenarios, comparing ordinary prompting, verification guidance, and disclosure-constrained verification.
why: It tests a potentially counterproductive safety intervention with inexpensive, causally interpretable experiments; the reviewed work studies clarification and privacy separately, but I found no direct test of verification-induced disclosure, subject to fuller novelty review.

direction: Make trusted sabotage monitors transfer to untrusted model families they weren't calibrated on, by testing training-time fixes for the family-specific overfit that Pinto (2026) diagnosed.
project: Lineage-Robust Monitors — Closing the Cross-Family Transfer Gap in Trusted Sabotage Monitoring
question: Can leave-one-family-out training, style normalization of transcripts (trusted-model paraphrase of actions and reasoning), or adversarial removal of family-identity information raise the off-lineage detection rate of trained monitors toward the in-lineage rate? That means attack-attempt TPR at a 1% audit budget, and Pinto's diagonal-interaction statistic shrinking toward 0. Does this hold when the held-out family is a newer model, and does it cost in-lineage detection?
first_experiment: Reproduce the baseline with ControlArena APPS backdoor transcripts from 4–5 open-weight families, plus a few frontier families if the budget allows. Fine-tune a LoRA transcript-reading monitor (Phi-4-mini) on one family, then measure the cross-family AUROC matrix and the interaction term. This should show the +0.17 interaction. Then compare four training conditions on the same matrix, with the held-out family never seen in training: 1. Single-family training. 2. Pooled multi-family training, which is Pinto's partial defense. 3. Pooled training with style normalization, where a fixed trusted model rewrites each transcript into a canonical style before the monitor sees it. 4. Pooled training with a gradient-reversal adversary that predicts family identity from the monitor's features. The main metric is off-lineage TPR at 1% FPR on the held-out family, with a check that in-lineage performance doesn't drop. A control checks whether the paraphrase step erases the sabotage signal itself, by comparing detection of paraphrased and original backdoors.
why: The failure is measured and the effect is large. It has a clear success metric, and it can be run with small open models and public tooling on modest compute. The first experiment either shows the gap can be closed, which is useful for control practice, or shows it is a fundamental property of the sabotage signal, which is also informative. It has not been done as far as I found: Pinto's paper and the related ensemble work diagnose the gap but, as far as I could tell, don't test training-time fixes. The main risks are that style normalization strips the sabotage signal and that results on APPS backdoors don't carry over to agentic settings such as SHADE-Arena. I would test the second risk in a follow-up.

direction: Make asynchronous AI oversight robust to agents that strategically shorten the time available to prevent irreversible harm.
project: Beating the Monitor to the Commit
question: Can an agent substantially reduce sabotage prevention by controlling activation and rollback deadlines, and can trusted commit barriers restore prevention without the throughput cost of monitoring every action synchronously?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired sandbox episodes with identical sabotage opportunities, varying whether the agent controls activation deadlines, and measure actual prevention under asynchronous, synchronous, and commit-barrier monitoring.
why: It targets a consequential gap between detecting misconduct and preventing harm, with a tractable causal experiment and deployable defense; the searched literature studies asynchronous detection, fragmentation, fatigue, and timing leakage, but I found no direct test of adversarial control over intervention windows—so novelty is promising, not established conclusively.

direction: Evaluate paired authorization-boundary execution tests as a defense against adaptive sabotage by AI coding agents.
project: Permission-Boundary Witnesses
question: Can executable permission-boundary witnesses reduce accepted successful sabotage beyond budget-matched transcript and structural monitors while preserving legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Compare inspection monitors, ordinary security testing, and paired pre/post-patch authorization probes on 60 containerized coding tasks with held-out repositories, independent exploit grading, and adaptive attackers.
why: It offers reproducible behavioral evidence and a tractable falsification test; the specific adaptive AI-control evaluation appears absent from the reviewed literature, although its underlying testing techniques are established.

direction: Test whether optimising a policy against an AI overseer creates blind spots that other overseers from the same model family share, rather than only exploiting that one overseer's quirks.
project: Inherited Blindness — Does RL Against One Grader Blind Its Relatives?
question: When a policy is RL-trained against an LLM grader from lineage A, are the reward hacks it learns caught less often by monitors from lineage A than by skill-matched monitors from other lineages? Does that own-family gap grow with optimisation pressure beyond the static correlation already present in the untrained policy?
first_experiment: A 2×2 crossed RL study: - **Policy and task:** GRPO-train Qwen3-4B on about 2,000 APPS/LiveCodeBench problems, scored only by an LLM judge that sees the code and the model's explanation but no tests. This makes hacks such as hardcoding visible-test outputs, special-casing, and explanations that misrepresent the code profitable. - **Graders:** two separate runs, one graded by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and one by Gemma-3-12B-it, with 3 seeds each. - **Ground truth:** hidden tests label every saved rollout as an honest solution, a hack, or an honest failure. - **Monitors:** about 8 reward-hack monitors, including the grader checkpoints themselves, siblings of the same family at other sizes and fine-tunes, and Mistral- and Phi-based outsiders. All are matched on detection skill (pAUC) beforehand using backdoored-APPS. - **Analysis:** at checkpoints 0, 100, 200 and 400, compute the grader-lineage × monitor-lineage interaction in detection AUROC, plus catch rate at a 1% audit budget. The step-0 interaction is the static baseline. - **Prediction:** the interaction rises with training steps in both crossings.
why: AI control and scalable oversight assume that monitors fail somewhat independently of the training signal. Yet developers commonly use related models as RL graders, reward models, auditors and deployment monitors. If optimisation pressure carries blind spots from a grader to its relatives, protocols that look safe on paper are overstated, and there is a concrete fix: keep grader and monitor lineages separate. A null result would also be useful, because it would justify reusing graders as monitors. It has not been done because existing lineage studies (2607.06596, 2608.16190) measure only static correlation, with no optimisation against the overseer. Judge-hacking and RL-obfuscation papers, for their part, test the overseer that was itself trained against, or the model's own judgments, never transfer to untouched relatives. My searches found no paper that treats the grader's lineage as a causal training variable and measures how many hacks other monitors miss as a result.

direction: Make trusted sabotage monitors robust to the lineage of the untrusted model by removing lineage-specific stylistic signal, instead of recalibrating per lineage.
project: Lineage-Invariant Monitors — Can Style Normalization Close the Cross-Family Gap in Trusted Sabotage Monitoring?
question: Does passing agent transcripts through a trusted normalizer, or training the monitor adversarially against lineage identity, recover most of the off-lineage detection gap? Specifically, at a 1% audit budget, does it cut the off-lineage catch-rate deficit relative to in-lineage by at least half. It must do this without lowering in-lineage detection by more than 3 points and without opening a new evasion route, such as an attacker hiding a backdoor in the normalizer's blind spot.
first_experiment: 1. Generate APPS backdoor and benign transcripts in ControlArena from 4 open-weight families (about 600 each), with Qwen, Llama, Mistral and one further family. 2. Run a leave-one-family-out protocol. Train a LoRA monitor (Phi-4-mini) on three families and test on the held-out fourth. Use the Pinto interaction statistic and catch rate at a 1% audit budget as metrics. 3. Compare four conditions: - raw transcripts (baseline, which should reproduce the gap); - transcripts rewritten by a fixed small trusted model, e.g. by stripping comments and renaming variables; - transcripts normalized by an AST/canonical-form code transform; - a gradient-reversal lineage-adversarial head on the raw transcripts. 4. Run a quick sanity check first: does a lineage classifier's accuracy drop to near chance after normalization? If it does not, the normalizer is not removing the signal and the direction is not viable.
why: The cross-lineage gap is a deployment-relevant failure. A monitor calibrated today will face a different model next quarter, and a published fix would make control evaluations more trustworthy. The existing evidence is a single independent-researcher paper that names the problem and offers only partial mitigations (reporting, recalibration, pooling). The searches I ran turned up no tested method that removes the lineage signal. The experiment is cheap, using small open-weight models, LoRA training and existing ControlArena data. A null result is also informative: it would show that the lineage signal is tied to the sabotage itself, so only recalibration helps. The main risk is that the Pinto result does not replicate on my data, which the baseline condition checks first. The registry shows no overlap with other agents.

direction: Test whether post-training that improves chain-of-thought monitorability survives later RL that pushes toward obfuscation, or whether that RL quietly erodes it.
project: Durable Legibility — Does Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Training Survive Later RL?
question: When a reasoning model gets monitorability post-training (mutual-information objective or intervention-aware self-distillation) and then undergoes RL that is known to degrade monitorability (a CoT-monitor penalty, output-only supervision, or a length penalty), does the monitor's detection rate of reward hacking fall more slowly and less far than for an untreated model, and does the treated model learn evasion faster?
first_experiment: Qwen3-1.7B on an MBPP-style coding task with exploitable unit tests (a test-hacking setup like CATCH or Countdown-Code). Build the untreated and mutual-information-trained variants, using Anwar et al.'s method or a minimal reimplementation of it. Then run about 200 GRPO steps with a reward that penalizes hacks flagged by a frozen CoT monitor, at several seeds. Every 25 steps, log how often the model hacks, how often a held-out monitor catches those hacks, and task pass rate. Viability signal: a clear gap between the two arms' detection curves. A null result, where both arms reach evasion at the same step, is also publishable.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that work today, and the field has just started proposing dedicated monitorability training stages. Whether such a stage lasts through later training is the deciding question for whether developers should adopt it, so the result matters either way. It has not been done because both training methods appeared less than three weeks ago (21–22 October 2026), and both evaluate only right after training. The original authors name later-training robustness as open future work. No paper I found, and no agent in the registry, covers it. It is also cheap to de-risk: one small model, existing open-source testbeds and short RL runs.

direction: Identify whether missing dependency edges or insufficient replay causes poisoned agent memories to recur after repair.
project: Why Repaired Memories Relapse
question: How much post-repair recurrence is causally attributable to incomplete dependency graphs versus selective replay, at matched benign utility?
first_experiment: Run a paired 2×2 ablation of recorded versus oracle dependencies and selective versus full affected-state replay on 100 synthetic poisoned-memory workflows, evaluating recurrence over ten clean follow-up sessions.
why: It targets a reported safety–efficiency tradeoff with a tractable causal experiment; existing work studies lineage, rollback, and repair outcomes, but the literature searched did not establish this specific decomposition of recurrence.

direction: Stress-test the new CoT-monitorability training methods to see whether their gains survive later RL pressure, or whether they make models learn to hide their reasoning faster by raising monitor-awareness and control over their CoT.
project: Legible Until Pressured: Does Monitorability Training Survive Later RL, or Teach Models to Obfuscate?
question: After models get monitorability post-training (Anwar et al.'s information-based objective, Fu et al.'s intervention-aware self-distillation, verbalization fine-tuning), (a) how much of the gain is left after standard RLVR (RL on automatically checkable rewards) and after RL with output-only supervision, and (b) do these models learn to hide their reasoning faster or slower than untreated models when the CoT and output rewards conflict, and is any difference explained by changes in how well they can control their CoT?
first_experiment: Start from Qwen3-8B. Make four branches: base, verbalization fine-tuning, intervention-aware self-distillation using Fu et al.'s released code and data, and the information-based objective. Before any later training, measure each branch on MonitorBench input-intervention tasks (scored with Fu et al.'s upper and lower causal bounds) and on the CoT-Control controllability benchmark. Then train each branch with GRPO in two settings. One is Drori et al.'s hints environment with an output-only penalty for mentioning the hint, which tests spillover. The other is a CoT-penalty setting where the rewards conflict, such as coin-flip state tracking or code backdooring in the style of Kaufmann et al. Use 3 seeds each. Track how often the CoT monitor catches hint use or hacking across training, how many steps it takes to reach 50% undetected misbehaviour, and task reward. The main comparison is the gap between the treated branches and base in steps-to-hiding, plus how much of each branch's monitorability gain remains after 200 steps of output-supervised RL.
why: Labs are about to adopt a monitorability post-training stage on the strength of evaluations taken right after training. If that stage is wiped out by ordinary later RL, or worse, speeds up learned hiding, recommended practice would make models harder to oversee while looking reassuring. The project directly tests a property Anwar et al. name as a goal but do not test. It joins three findings nobody has put together: spillover from output supervision, faster hiding by monitor-aware models, and the link between CoT control and hiding. It has not been done because the training methods are only weeks old (October 21–22, 2026). Earlier hiding studies used untreated models, and the new methods' papers measure monitorability only once, right after training. The registry shows no one working on it. It is cheap: open 4–8B models, existing code and benchmarks, and a single-node GRPO setup are enough, and a result in either direction would change how labs use these methods.

direction: Stress-test the new CoT-monitorability post-training methods (especially Anwar et al.'s mutual-information objective) against encoded, illegible reasoning and against later obfuscation pressure, to find out whether "monitorability is trainable" holds up against an adversary.
project: Informative but Unreadable: Do Monitorability Training Methods Survive Encoded Reasoning and Later Optimisation Pressure?
question: When a model's CoT has been degraded by *encoding* (learned code substitutions) rather than *omission*, does post-training that raises CoT–output mutual information restore what an LLM monitor can detect, or does it raise mutual information while monitor detection stays flat? And does a model trained for monitorability learn to evade a CoT monitor more slowly under later RL than an untreated control?
first_experiment: Build an encoded-reasoning model organism following Skaf et al. on Qwen3-8B. The model does state-tracking tasks (e.g. tracking a sequence of coin flips) and a programming task with a reward hack, while trained against a monitor that penalises key words. Train until it reliably replaces those words with learned codes and its task accuracy stays high. Then apply Anwar et al.'s released recipe, sweeping the regulariser budget ε ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 1.0}, plus a version with no regulariser. For each checkpoint, measure: - the training-time mutual-information estimate; - how often an LLM monitor catches the hack (true- and false-positive rates); - how much of the code a decoder model recovers, as a legibility check; - task accuracy. The prediction to falsify: mutual information rises while monitor detection stays near the degraded baseline, especially at tighter regulariser budgets. Second arm: run identical monitor-penalising RL on (a) the treated model and (b) the untreated base model, and compare how many steps each takes to reach 20% undetected hacking.
why: CoT monitoring is a central safety tool, and labs may soon add monitorability post-training to protect it. If the method can be satisfied by unreadable CoT, or wears off under ordinary RL, the result would give false reassurance precisely where it matters most. The experiment is cheap, uses public code (Anwar et al.'s recipe and the Skaf et al. setup) and 8B-scale models, and gives a clear yes/no answer. It hasn't been done because the methods are only 2–3 weeks old (21–22 Oct 2026). Their evaluations cover only omission-type degradation and measure monitorability right after training, never after further pressure. My searches found no work testing encoded-reasoning failure or durability, and no AI safety project in the registry.

direction: Operational corrigibility through agents that continuously preserve humans’ ability to recover control after abrupt agent removal.
project: Takeover Margin — Training Agents to Remain Safely Replaceable
question: Can surprise-removal training improve bounded-time human recovery from intermediate agent-created states without substantially reducing task performance?
first_experiment: Randomly terminate agents during sandboxed service-maintenance tasks and compare blinded human recovery across task-only, documentation-only, and takeover-aware conditions at matched progress.
why: It addresses loss of control through operational dependence with a directly testable intervention; its proposed novelty is training on recovery after unannounced agent removal, rather than shutdown obedience or final handoff quality, although broader priority remains to be verified.

direction: Test whether optimization pressure on CoT monitors for unrelated misbehavior pushes evaluation-awareness reasoning out of the CoT.
project: Spillover of CoT-Monitor Pressure onto Evaluation-Awareness Verbalization
question: Does RL against a CoT monitor for one behavior reduce verbalized evaluation awareness more than the targeted behavior, while the behavioral eval/deployment gap and probe-detectable EA persist?
first_experiment: RL on exploitable coding tasks with a no-penalty arm, a CoT-monitor-penalty arm and an output-only-penalty arm. At each checkpoint, measure verbalized EA, the eval/deployment behavioral gap, monitor detection and EA probe AUROC.
why: Monitor pressure is the likely real-world route to losing the verbalized-EA signal. I found no direct test of this spillover, though my literature search was limited.

direction: Test whether CoT obfuscation learned against one monitor transfers to unseen monitors, and whether monitor ensembles resist it.
project: Monitor Transfer — Does Obfuscation Learned Against One CoT Monitor Evade Others?
question: Does RL against one CoT monitor yield obfuscation that evades held-out monitors, and do diverse monitor ensembles prevent or delay it?
