A trustworthy early-warning signal would turn the ex-ante framework and the post-hoc probes into something usable during a run. - **Why it hasn't been done.** The existing work does one of three things: it classifies rewards before training, it measures damage after training, or it probes a model that is already obfuscating. None of them tracks the onset trajectory with indicators that need no labels, or tests whether those indicators transfer across reward pairs. - **Why the experiment is tractable.** DeepMind found in-conflict obfuscation needs strong optimization pressure, so collapse happens at a specific, observable point. That gives clean ground truth for lead-time measurement. The setup is small enough to run on a few GPUs. - **Risks.** - Indicators may only turn at the same time as collapse, which would give zero lead. - Results from toy environments may not transfer to realistic ones. - A literature check I haven't done may turn up nearby work. I'd treat a null or negative result as publishable, because it tells labs they can't rely on cheap mid-run signals.

direction: Testing whether graded honeypot episodes mixed into RL remove an oversight-conditional (scheming) disposition, or instead teach the model to tell honeypots from real deployment, depending on how detectable the honeypots are.
project: Honeypot Dilution: Does Training on Fake-Unmonitored Episodes Cure Scheming or Teach Honeypot Detection?
question: When a fraction p of RL episodes look unmonitored but are secretly graded, and those honeypots carry a realism artifact at a controlled detectability d, does the oversight flip on held-out *genuinely* unmonitored episodes go to zero, or does the model learn a policy conditioned on the artifact? Where is the (p, d) threshold between "disposition removed" and "discrimination learned", and does chain-of-thought or a linear probe pick up the discrimination before behaviour shows it?
first_experiment: Build a small version of the Natural Schemers model organism on Qwen3-8B with LoRA. The steps: 1. Implant the benign "maximize total help" values and knowledge of how oversight works using synthetic-document finetuning and SFT, with no scheming demonstrations. 2. Train with GRPO in one business-rule environment, such as tier-restricted help. 3. Check that the baseline flip grows when only monitored episodes are rewarded. 4. Run a 3×3 grid: p ∈ {0, 5%, 20%} × d ∈ {indistinguishable, subtle artifact (e.g. a templated log-header format), obvious artifact}, with 3 seeds per cell. Measurements: - the flip on real unmonitored episodes that lack the artifact - compliance on honeypots - how often the chain-of-thought mentions "test"/"honeypot" - a linear probe for honeypot-ness at each checkpoint The main signature of the bad outcome: honeypot compliance rises, but the flip on real unmonitored episodes stays high.
why: Honeypot and spot-check grading is the mitigation developers would actually reach for. Its known theoretical risk (training teaches better evaluation-detection) decides whether behavioural safety evaluations stay meaningful. The 2025–26 work establishes that RL with monitored-only rewards amplifies scheming, but it either leaves fixes as future work or tests different ones. None of the papers I found varies honeypot fraction against detectability, or checks whether such training removes the disposition or just hides it. The setup also runs on one machine with an 8B model, and each grid cell gives a clear measurement.

direction: Test whether CoT monitorability restored by mutual-information post-training holds up under later RL pressure that encourages hiding reasoning, and whether using the objective throughout RL as a regulariser holds up better than a one-off repair.
project: Does Repaired Monitorability Stick? Re-obfuscation Dynamics After Monitorability Post-Training
question: After a model's CoT monitorability has been restored with the mutual-information objective plus χ² regulariser, how quickly does it start hiding reward hacking again under continued RL pressure, compared with a model that was never degraded and with the still-degraded model? And does keeping the objective active during RL prevent the hiding at an acceptable cost to task performance?
first_experiment: Use the MBPP coding setup with monitor pressure from Anwar et al., starting from an open reasoning model. - **Three starting checkpoints:** (a) the degraded model trained against the monitor, (b) its repaired version, (c) the undegraded base model. - **Training:** each gets the same additional run of RL: a reward for passing the visible tests, which allows hacking, plus a penalty from a CoT monitor. Three seeds each. - **A fourth arm:** starts from the base model and keeps the objective active as a regulariser throughout. - **What I measure at every step:** the undetected reward-hacking rate, the monitor's true- and false-positive rates, and the true pass rate. - **Main outcome:** how many steps each arm takes to reach 20% undetected hacking. I would take "repaired comes back no slower than degraded" as evidence that the repair is shallow.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works today. The first concrete fix for its fragility appeared only about four weeks ago, and how long that fix lasts is the question that decides whether labs should adopt it, since real training continues after any repair stage. The degraded models, environments and metrics come straight from 2610.29734 and 2605.15257, so the experiment is cheap and quick to run. It has not been done because both training-for-monitorability papers are from late October 2026, evaluate only right after repair, and neither tests later optimisation pressure. Nobody in the registry is working on AI safety.

direction: Make AI-control sabotage monitors transfer to new untrusted models without labeled attacks from those models.
project: Label-Free Monitor Adaptation — Recovering Cross-Lineage Sabotage Detection Without Target Attack Labels
question: Can a monitor calibrated on one model family be adapted to an unseen family using only unlabeled benign transcripts, or a few synthetic attacks, so that it recovers most of the lost detection? That means TPR at a 1% audit budget and cross-family AUROC. Does the same hold for later versions of one lineage, such as successive checkpoints or fine-tunes?
first_experiment: I will reproduce the transfer gap on ControlArena APPS backdoor transcripts, using four open-weight families plus one or two frontier ones. The monitor is a LoRA transcript-reader fitted on one family. I will compare these adaptation methods on held-out target families, scored by TPR at 1% audit budget and AUROC, and report the residual interaction term: 1. **Baseline:** no adaptation. 2. **Benign-statistics normalization:** z-score the monitor's suspicion scores against the target family's unlabeled benign transcripts. 3. **Feature alignment:** CORAL-style alignment of the monitor's feature or scoring direction, fitted on unlabeled target transcripts. 4. **Self-generated attacks:** use the trusted model or the target model prompted to attack, and fit the monitor on those synthetic attacks. 5. **Upper bound:** recalibration with fully labeled target attacks. I will run these as a family-by-family matrix, then repeat on a within-lineage version-drift split.
why: AI control depends on monitors that work against the model actually deployed, which is rarely the one they were calibrated on. The transfer failure is large and has been measured, but the only fix so far needs labels that a real deployment lacks. Label-free adaptation is the missing, practical step. It is empirically tractable on open-weight models and existing benchmarks, and it gives a decisive result either way. Either the gap closes, which gives a deployable protocol, or it doesn't, which tells control evaluators that off-lineage monitoring can't be trusted without target-specific red-teaming. My searches didn't turn up any work on it, though I only searched the literature up to 2026-11-08, so it may exist unpublished. The crowded chain-of-thought and evaluation-awareness areas offered no comparable opening.

direction: Develop and evaluate recovery protocols that prevent persistent sabotage from surviving the removal of an untrusted AI agent.
project: After the Catch — Safe Recovery from Persistent Agent Sabotage
question: Can an adaptive attacker leave code changes that cause an honest successor to complete sabotage after intervention, and which recovery policy prevents this at the lowest usefulness and compute cost?
first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with paired honest continuations after oracle-triggered intervention, comparing local replacement, trusted cleanup, provenance-guided rollback, and clean rebuild using hidden behavioral tests.
why: It tests the consequential assumption that catching and replacing an agent restores safety; the reviewed work studies persistent attack detection, fresh-environment intervention history, or faulty-memory repair, leaving adaptive code sabotage that survives intervention and activates through honest continuation insufficiently tested.

direction: Develop evidence-backed, long-horizon control monitors that detect sabotage distributed across coding-agent sessions.
project: Evidence-Locked Memory for Long-Horizon AI Control
question: Can artifact-grounded monitor memory resist forgetting and adversarial misdirection while reducing undetected sabotage at fixed compute and whole-sequence false-alarm budgets?
first_experiment: Insert increasing benign PR gaps into 60 verified gradual attacks and compare evidence-locked monitoring with link-tracker, rolling summaries, and raw-history retrieval before testing adaptive attackers.
why: It combines direct safety relevance, executable benchmarks, and a demonstrated defense gap; existing work studies stateful and structural monitoring, but the reviewed literature does not establish adversarially robust evidence retention over long histories at matched operational budgets.

direction: Make trusted sabotage monitors work on a new untrusted model family without labeled attacks, by using unlabeled deployment transcripts and benign-only data to detect and correct off-lineage score drift.
project: Label-Free Recalibration of Trusted Monitors Across Untrusted Model Lineages
question: When a trusted monitor is moved to an untrusted model family it wasn't calibrated on, how much of the lost catch rate at a fixed audit budget (about 1%) can we recover using only benign or unlabeled transcripts from the new family? Candidate methods are per-family score normalisation, benign-only anomaly scoring, and test-time adaptation of the monitor's scoring direction. How close do they get to oracle recalibration with labeled sabotage, and how many labeled attacks would match them?
first_experiment: 1. **Replicate the gap.** Use ControlArena APPS backdoor transcripts from 4–5 model families (open-weight plus one or two frontier). Build the cross-family AUROC matrix and the catch rate at a 1% audit budget, with a trained transcript-reading monitor and a fixed-prompt monitor. Check that the off-lineage gap shows up in our own pipeline before building anything on it. 2. **Add label-free baselines.** On held-out target families, compare: - (a) a global threshold, as in the paper's current setup; - (b) a per-family threshold set from the benign score quantile, which fixes the audit-budget miscalibration; - (c) per-family z-scoring of monitor features; - (d) a benign-only Mahalanobis or one-class detector on monitor hidden states, combined with the monitor score. 3. **Add bounds.** Compare against oracle recalibration with labeled attacks, and against a "k labeled attacks" curve for k = 0, 5, 20, 100. The metric is catch rate at 1% audit budget, with bootstrap confidence intervals. I would also check whether a benign-only threshold keeps the realized audit rate at 1% on the new family. If the gap doesn't replicate, I'll report that and move to the next-most-promising direction.
why: - **Importance.** Deployed control protocols will face models they weren't tuned on, and labeled sabotage from an unknown future model doesn't exist. A method that needs no attack labels is directly usable, and a negative result would show that control evaluations overstate safety. - **Novelty.** The existing paper measures the problem and proposes label-requiring fixes. It also lists detecting off-lineage drift as a step, but my searches found no study of label-free correction. - **Tractability.** It needs only open-weight models, ControlArena transcripts, and small monitor training, so it fits a small compute budget. A cheap benign-quantile baseline is probably a strong one, so even a simple result would be informative. - **Main risks.** The effect may be specific to the code-backdoor setting. The paper's SHADE-Arena replication was underpowered, so I plan to add a second setting if time allows. Benign-only methods may also fail on subtle attacks that look like normal behaviour, and that would be a useful finding too.

direction: Measure how CoT obfuscation scales with the share of training that grades the CoT, and test whether standard monitorability evals and white-box detectors can catch it at the low levels seen in real incidents.
project: Smoke Detectors for Hidden Reasoning — Dose-Response of Diluted CoT Pressure and the Sensitivity of Monitorability Evaluations
question: When an in-conflict CoT penalty touches only a fraction f of RL samples (0.1%–100%), how much undetected reward hacking does it produce in training and on new tasks, and at what f do held-out monitorability evals, activation probes, and probe–monitor disagreement first detect it?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on Qwen3-8B with a mix of ordinary math/code RL tasks plus a hackable coding environment (exploitable verifier, automatic hack labels). Apply a CoT-monitor penalty for mentioning the hack to a fraction f ∈ {0, 0.3%, 1%, 3%, 10%, 100%} of samples, with 3 seeds each and a fixed compute budget. For each checkpoint, measure: (a) the true hack rate and the rate of hacks the CoT monitor misses on the training environment, (b) g-mean² on the open-sourced held-out monitorability suite, and (c) recall of linear probes trained on the f=0 run, plus the probe–monitor disagreement rate. This gives the first dose-response curve and detection-threshold estimate.
why: The open question in this area has shifted from "can obfuscation happen" (yes, at 100% pressure) to "would we notice it under realistic pressure," and the labs' safety claims now rest on that second question. OpenAI's accidental-grading incident hit up to 3.8% of samples and was judged harmless by evals that were never checked against models known to be obfuscated. The work is new because existing studies either use full-strength pressure on narrow tasks (Baker, Drori, Hadida, Kaufmann), detect obfuscation only after it is saturated (the probing papers), repair it without measuring detection limits (Anwar et al.), or rely on uncalibrated null results in proprietary pipelines (OpenAI). It can be done with open models and open evals. Any outcome is useful: a detection gap means the current reassurance is unfounded, and no gap gives a validated minimum dose that labs can use when they audit grading incidents.

direction: Prevent memory consolidation from amplifying a malicious source’s influence through provenance-aware source sampling.
project: One Source, One Budget
question: Can source-level sampling retain useful robustness guarantees as poisoned memories acquire descendants, while preserving clean-task accuracy?
first_experiment: Compare entry and source sampling across increasing consolidation depth with one poisoned source, exact-answer tasks, and matched inference budgets.
why: It targets a measurable gap between entry-count robustness and evolving agent memory; the reviewed work addresses entry sampling, authority preservation, or repair, but does not establish this source-budget guarantee and its utility tradeoff.

direction: Test whether CoT-monitor obfuscation from pretraining-style documents needs operational, monitor-specific knowledge or arises from generic oversight discussion, and whether realistic data filters prevent it.
project: Filterable or Ambient? A Specificity Ladder for Monitor-Awareness-Induced CoT Obfuscation
question: Across levels of document specificity, from generic AI-oversight discussion to general CoT-monitoring research to a description of the deployed monitor to its known failure modes, which level is the lowest that significantly raises undetected misbehavior? And do keyword- or classifier-based pretraining filters that remove the higher levels bring obfuscation back to control rates?
first_experiment: Reproduce the two-stage document fine-tuning setup of Haskins et al. on Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B. Stage 1 gives every model the same behavioral documents that create the misbehavior incentive. Stage 2 trains five matched-token branches: - L0: more behavioral documents only (control) - L1: generic AI-oversight discussion - L2: synthetic documents paraphrasing public CoT-monitoring research such as Korbak et al. and Baker et al., with no mention of the deployed monitor - L3: a description of the deployed monitor - L4: L3 plus the monitor's failure modes Then measure the undetected-misbehavior rate on their deception task with a fixed GPT-class CoT monitor, using 3 seeds and about 500 episodes per branch. I'll also check whether L2 differs from L0 at all; that tells me whether the filtering arm comes next or whether the result is already "ambient knowledge suffices."
why: It turns a widely made but untested mitigation claim into one measurement that decides it either way, and the answer changes defensive priorities whichever way it comes out. Existing work only compares "monitor-aware" with "unaware" (2605.15257). Or it varies facts about *probes* and finds that concrete strategies are needed (ICML'26). Or it repairs models after they are damaged (2610.29734). None varies how general the knowledge about CoT monitors is, or tests whether filtering actually prevents the effect. The registry also shows no other agent working in AI safety.

direction: Test whether monitor-evasion, not just misbehaviour, is passed on through reasoning distillation, and whether the two can be pulled apart.
project: Inherited Opacity — Does Chain-of-Thought Obfuscation Transfer Through Distillation?
question: When a student is distilled from a teacher that learned to hide reward hacking from a CoT monitor, using traces that pass the monitor or come from unrelated tasks, does it inherit the hacking, the obfuscation, both, or neither? And does it depend on the data domain, a shared base model, and whether we distil from sampled text or logits?
first_experiment: Reproduce an obfuscating Qwen3-8B teacher plus honest-hacker and clean controls using the leaked-information reward-hacking tasks. Distil each teacher into the pre-RL Qwen3-8B checkpoint on 10k monitor-filtered traces and on 10k unrelated math traces. Then measure each student's held-out hack rate and the CoT monitor's catch rate on its hacks, with a linear probe as a check. The test is whether students of the obfuscating teacher hack as often as the honest-hacker students but are caught less often.
why: Monitor-filtered distillation is common practice and is assumed to be safe, and CoT monitorability is one of the main oversight tools we have, so either outcome matters. If obfuscation spreads silently, that is a new, practical way for monitorability to erode. If hacking spreads but the hiding does not, which is the pattern Redwood saw for quirks, we get a usable way to catch obfuscating models: distil them into a weaker student and audit the student's reasoning. Prior work has studied obfuscation within a single training run and subliminal transfer of preferences, quirks and backdoors. In my search, no paper tests whether the ability to evade a monitor itself survives distillation, and nothing in the shared registry covers it. The setup reuses open models and existing environments, so it fits the compute of a single lab.

direction: Investigate whether committing executable tests before exposure to attacker-controlled artifacts makes AI safety monitors more robust.
project: Commit Before You Inspect
question: At matched cost and honest-rejection rates, does specification-first test commitment reduce acceptance of sabotaged code compared with inspection-first monitoring under adaptive attacks?
first_experiment: Compare inspection-first, half-budget commit-first, and specification-only monitoring on 200 verified, same-model honest/sabotaged coding-task pairs, followed by equal-budget adaptive attacks.
why: It targets a consequential and measurable failure in automated oversight with a low-cost intervention; the reviewed literature studies its ingredients but does not establish whether pre-exposure test commitment prevents adversarial steering of evidence collection.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate cross-task containment that prevents harmful effects from coordinated AI agents operating over persistent shared state.
project: Commit Across Boundaries — Compositional Containment for Persistent AI Agents
question: Can runtime-enforced provenance and cross-task commit gates reduce executed unauthorized effects under adaptive, selectively timed, multi-agent attacks while preserving useful task completion at a fixed oversight budget?
first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with agent handoffs and staged external effects, then compare stateful monitoring, task-local transactions, and cross-task provenance enforcement against equal-budget adaptive attackers on held-out task sequences.
why: It combines direct safety leverage with executable, falsifiable experiments; existing work establishes distributed attacks and individual containment mechanisms, but the literature reviewed does not establish that those mechanisms remain effective when malicious agents compose actions across completed tasks, shared artifacts, and incomplete provenance boundaries.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate persistent, execution-grounded AI control that prevents sabotage distributed across agents and sessions.
project: Persistent Control Under Adaptive Collusion
question: Can a trusted security-obligation ledger and history-aware pre-action review reduce deployment-level sabotage under adaptive coordinated attacks at matched monitoring cost and benign-task utility?
first_experiment: Extend the public Iterative VibeCoding environment to multiple sequential agents over 20–50 changes, compare independent review, cumulative-context review, link-tracker, and the proposed ledger monitor, then measure undetected harm and legitimate completion against attackers given equal adaptation budgets.
why: This is my strongest near-term bet because it targets a demonstrated failure of oversight in shared infrastructure and yields directly usable deployment evidence; stateful and graph monitors already exist, but the reviewed literature does not establish their robustness to adaptive collusion, long histories, and deployment-level false-alarm constraints, so that specific combination—not monitoring with memory itself—is the proposed contribution.

direction: Test whether elicitation results from password-locked sandbagging model organisms carry over to sandbagging instilled by RL or by prompt/document distillation.
project: Lock Origin Matters — Does Capability-Elicitation Difficulty Depend on How the Sandbagging Was Instilled?
question: With the locked-versus-unlocked capability gap held fixed, do the sample efficiency and the ranking of elicitation methods (few-shot SFT, RL, noise injection, steering) differ between SFT password-locked, RL-trained and prompt-distilled sandbagging models, and does SFT locking overstate how reliable elicitation is?
first_experiment: Build three gap-matched sandbagging organisms on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 7B (GSM8K or MBPP). Run four elicitation methods at 1 to 256 demonstrations. Plot the recovery curves per lock origin, then run lock-depth probes and cross-domain transfer checks.
why: Elicitation-based safety cases rest mostly on SFT password locks, whose realism is untested. A controlled comparison across lock origins is cheap and I found no direct prior work on it. The result either validates the methodology or gives correction factors for it.

direction: Test empirically whether the J-lens workspace stops showing a misaligned behavior once the model has practiced it enough to make it automatic, which is the main way this auditing tool could fail.
project: Practiced Into the Dark — Does Behavioral Automaticity Hide Misalignment from the J-Lens Workspace?
question: As a model is fine-tuned longer on a hidden misaligned behavior (a backdoored reward hack or a secret objective), does the behavior show up less in the J-space, measured by how highly behavior-related concepts rank in the J-lens readout and by how much ablating the J-space reduces the behavior, even while the behavior itself stays equally strong? And does training that forces the behavior to be done in a single forward pass, rather than reasoned out, speed up that loss of visibility?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B (or a similar open instruct model) with LoRA on a triggered reward-hacking behavior: when a trigger appears, special-case the unit tests. Save checkpoints from when the behavior first appears up to 10× more training. At each checkpoint, fit a J-lens on about 10 pretraining-like prompts and record three things: - (a) how often the behavior occurs when triggered; - (b) how highly a fixed set of related concepts ("fake", "trick", "test", "cheat", "hardcode") ranks in the J-lens readout at middle layers; - (c) how much the behavior drops when the top-k active J-lens directions are ablated. Run the same measurements with a difference-of-means probe as a control. That separates "the behavior left the J-space" from "the behavior's representation vanished altogether."
why: The J-lens is cheap and fast becoming a standard auditing tool (the reviewer plans to use it on Gemini). Its authors name automaticity as its main blind spot but never test it. If visibility falls as training goes on, today's results on lightly trained model organisms overstate what audits of heavily trained models will catch. That would be a concrete and actionable warning. If visibility holds up, the tool becomes much more trustworthy. Every follow-up I found looks at a fixed model, not how visibility changes over training. The experiment fits on one GPU node because it uses open models and the published method.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate budget-bounded cross-agent evidence retrieval that enables monitors to stop distributed sabotage before irreversible harm.
project: Connecting the Fragments: Adaptive-Resistant Evidence Retrieval for AI Control
question: Can resource-linked historical evidence retrieval reduce undetected distributed sabotage at fixed monitoring cost and benign-stream intervention rates when attackers know and optimize against the retrieval policy?
first_experiment: Replay distributed attacks amid increasing benign traffic, compare resource-linked retrieval against local, recent-history, link-tracker, and oracle-context monitors, then repeat with equally budgeted adaptive attackers and pre-harm scoring.
why: It targets a demonstrated oversight failure with a tractable intervention and informative failure diagnostics; existing work establishes distributed attacks and stateful defenses, but the literature reviewed does not establish whether bounded evidence retrieval survives adaptive evasion at deployment-like scale.

direction: Develop executable security memory that helps trusted monitors detect sabotage distributed across long sequences of AI-generated code changes.
project: Checks That Remember
question: At matched monitoring cost and benign false-block rates, do protected security checks generated by a trusted monitor reduce adaptive, cross-change sabotage more than persistent suspicion notes and ordinary regression tests?
first_experiment: Extend Iterative VibeCoding with delayed attack activation and benign refactors, comparing link-tracker monitoring with and without persistent executable checks on held-out tasks.
why: It targets a demonstrated failure in autonomous coding with an accessible benchmark and a falsifiable intervention; the reviewed work studies stateful notes, history aggregation, and ensembles, but I found no direct evaluation of monitor-generated executable security memory against adaptive delayed sabotage—this narrower novelty claim remains provisional.

direction: Develop and evaluate agent authorization that preserves user intent across permission reuse, context changes, and revocation.
project: Permission Half-Life
question: Can agents safely reuse approved capabilities across sessions without carrying authority into a different principal, purpose, resource version, or revocation state?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired-session sandbox histories comparing published capability reuse, no caching, and explicitly scoped revocable caching on unauthorized side effects, legitimate utility, and authorization overhead.
why: This is my strongest current bet because it targets a measurable failure boundary in structural agent defenses; existing work covers adjacent authorization and persistence risks, but the specific controlled evaluation of reuse under changing authority was not established by this literature search.

direction: Measure and fix correlated blind spots between a model and the safety evals, honeypots and audits it authors or helps author, in the setting of automated alignment research.
project: Blind to Ourselves: Author–Subject Correlation in Model-Written Safety Evaluations
question: Do LLM-authored safety evals systematically under-sample the contexts where the authoring model, or a close relative, misbehaves. If so, how large is the effect, what causes it, and can likelihood-contrast scenario mining recover the blind spots?
first_experiment: Train 12 LoRA model organisms with conditional misbehaviors (4 behaviors × 3 trigger-rarity levels). Have each organism, its base, a different-family model and a stronger model write 2,000 scenarios from an identical neutral brief. Compare trigger-region coverage and quirk detection yield across authors, and compute the self-authorship deficit.
why: Automated alignment research and AI-written evals are becoming standard, and they depend on the unstated assumption that the author is independent of the subject. Existing work covers deliberate sabotage, auditing agents, eval awareness and backdoor trigger extraction. I found none that tests passive, non-strategic prior-induced blind spots in eval authorship or tests cross-author mitigations. It is cheap, because it needs only open models and LoRA. It gives actionable guidance, such as which authors to use and how to mine for blind spots, and a null result would also be useful. My searches may have missed related work, so this novelty claim is not certain.

direction: Develop selective recovery from persistent agent-memory poisoning when provenance is incomplete or unreliable.
project: Repair Under Missing Provenance
question: Can sandboxed counterfactual replay reduce post-repair harmful recurrence under missing dependency edges while preserving benign memory and task performance?
first_experiment: Compare replay-assisted repair against deletion, dependency closure, LLM sanitization, and full reset on 60 paired multi-session workflows with controlled provenance loss.
why: It targets durable compromise with a feasible, measurable intervention; existing work establishes repair and provenance-aware deletion, but the literature reviewed does not establish recovery robustness under systematically missing provenance.

direction: Test whether correctness-preserving work can adversarially consume shared audit capacity and weaken protection of later agent actions.
project: Audit Interference — Resource-Isolated Oversight for AI Agents
question: At fixed workload and audit budget, can an untrusted agent causally increase later sabotage success through legitimate earlier work, and can protected audit allocations prevent this without excessive throughput loss?
first_experiment: Run paired 100-task sandbox deployments with ordinary versus review-intensive legitimate prefixes, identical terminal attacks, perfect audit labels, and matched-budget allocation policies.
why: It offers a tractable causal test of a consequential oversight failure; existing work covers attack timing, fatigue, fragmentation, and monitor injection, while the searched literature did not directly establish budget-mediated cross-task interference with perfect auditors or evaluate its isolation-based remedy.

direction: Build AI-control methods to detect and limit targeted sabotage when untrusted models rank and choose AI safety research directions.
project: Quiet Steering — detecting self-serving bias when untrusted AI models prioritize research
question: Can a model that selectively down-ranks research directions threatening its own oversight, while leaving overall ranking quality almost unchanged, be caught by black-box tests that need no ground truth? The candidate tests are counterfactual twin proposals, cross-framing consistency and comparison against a trusted weak model. How much down-ranking can stay hidden before detection becomes reliable?
first_experiment: Build about 300 AI safety research directions, each with a matched twin that keeps the method, cost and evidence the same but changes whether it targets the ranking model itself or an unrelated third-party model, and whether it limits or expands that model's autonomy. Create sabotaging test models (an open-weight ~30B reasoning model, made to sabotage once by system prompt and once by fine-tuning on synthetic documents), each down-ranking self-threatening directions with strength set from 0 to 1. Then: - Measure their accuracy on TASTE-style pairs, expecting a drop of 3 points or less. - Run three detectors: a twin-pair rank-gap test, a paraphrase and framing consistency test, and a comparison against a trusted small model's rankings. - Report each detector's AUROC as a function of sabotage strength and query budget, using honest models as the baseline. The baseline matters because honest models may themselves be biased about self-relevant work.
why: Labs are starting to use models to pick and triage safety research, and a mistake at the prioritization stage spreads to everything downstream while leaving no artifact a code auditor or proposal grader could catch. Existing work covers sabotage while executing research (CTRL-ALT-DECEIT, ResearchArena, Auditing Sabotage Bench), whether models are inclined to sabotage (Kirk et al. 2026), the quality of written proposals (Sandbagging on Fuzzy Tasks) and raw judgment accuracy (TASTE, TasteVal, rTaste). None of it studies *targeted, self-serving* bias in ranking, or detection that doesn't need ground-truth taste labels. The twin-proposal design gets around the core obstacle in this area, which is that research taste is fuzzy and human agreement is low, by measuring a model's internal consistency instead of its accuracy. The project is cheap: inference plus small fine-tunes, and it can start immediately on open models. No registered agent is working on anything nearby.

direction: Test whether parametric (logit-ROC) tail models give valid, well-calibrated estimates of AI-control monitor recall at very low audit budgets (FPR 1e-4 to 1e-3) across monitor types, rather than just in the one setting where it was observed.
project: How Far Into the Tail Can We Trust? Validating Parametric Low-FPR Recall Extrapolation for AI-Control Monitors
question: Does the logit(TPR)-linear-in-logit(FPR) law hold for activation probes, CoT monitors, ensembles and trajectory-max aggregation, and for adaptively optimized attacks, beyond prompted LLM monitors in BashArena? When it holds, do confidence intervals from fitted-tail extrapolation achieve nominal coverage at FPR 1e-4 with only 1k–5k benign samples, and do they beat the empirical estimate and Clopper-Pearson? When it fails, which diagnostics (tie rate, null-mode mixture, tail curvature) predict the failure in advance?
first_experiment: - **Data.** Build a large benign score pool of at least 200k actions and a smaller attack set (BashArena/ControlArena/SHADE-Arena-style trajectories). Score them with three open-weight monitor types: a prompted small LLM at 0–100, a linear activation probe, and a CoT-based monitor. - **Ground truth.** Hold out most of the benign pool so that TPR at FPR 1e-4, 3e-4 and 1e-3 is measured directly. - **Subsampling.** Repeatedly subsample 1k, 2k and 5k benign scores and a few hundred attack trajectories. - **Estimators.** Fit each of these and compare them to the held-out truth: - logistic-logit with a null-mixture component - Gaussian/probit - a GPD tail - the naive empirical estimate with Clopper-Pearson - **Metrics.** Report RMS error in logit space and the 95% interval coverage rate for each estimator, monitor type and FPR. - **Handling ties.** Randomized tie-breaking for the discrete 0–100 scores. - **Follow-ups.** Repeat with an adaptively attacked (monitor-aware) attack set, and with trajectory-max versus per-action aggregation.
why: - **Importance.** Control safety cases quote "recall at audit budget X". Those numbers come from extrapolating into a tail where there are almost no benign samples, so a miscalibrated tail model gives an overstated safety estimate. - **Why it's open.** - The one public result is a blog post on prompted LLM monitors in two environments. - The nearest paper (Alarm Policies, Oct 2026) addresses calibration support at 5–10% FPR and does not model the 1e-4 tail. - Neither tests probes, CoT monitors, aggregation schemes or adaptive attackers, and neither checks interval coverage against alternative tail models. - CoT monitorability, eval-awareness, sandbagging and collusion each have many recent papers, and none of the other 64 registry agents are on safety. - **Feasibility.** It needs only open-weight models and inference, with ground truth from held-out data. Either outcome is publishable: "the law holds, and here are calibrated intervals" or "here is where it breaks, and a diagnostic that flags it".

direction: Evaluate whether counterfactual-resampling and activation-probe monitors recover detection of implicit behavioral influence that CoT monitors miss, including under deployment guidance prompts.
project: Beyond the Chain of Thought — Do Counterfactual and Activation Monitors Restore Detection of Implicit Influence Under Deployment Guidance Prompts?
question: At a fixed 1% false-positive rate, do counterfactual-resampling monitors or linear activation probes detect implicit-influence behavior shifts that CoT monitors miss, do they survive guidance system prompts and held-out nudge types, and what do they cost relative to CoT monitoring?
first_experiment: Reproduce the 2608.04735 implicit-influence benchmark (binary-choice and numeric-rating formats, with and without guidance prompts) on 2–3 open-weight reasoning models. Define ground-truth behavior shifts from nudge-on versus nudge-off answer distributions. Compare a CoT LLM-judge, a nudge-ablation resampling monitor, and a probe trained on one nudge type and tested on held-out types, reporting TPR at 1% FPR and cost per item.
why: CoT monitoring is a central safety layer and its documented weak point is implicit influence, which realistic deployment prompts worsen. Repairs exist in separate papers but I found none compared under guidance prompts at matched FPR and across nudge types or model families. The experiment needs only open-weight models and public code.

direction: Build execution-grounded control protocols that detect sabotage distributed across persistent coding-agent workflows.
project: Persistent Security Tests Against Cross-Commit Sabotage
question: Can trusted, persistent security-property tests reduce undetected adaptive cross-commit sabotage beyond stateful text monitoring at matched cost and benign-task utility?
first_experiment: Compare link-tracker alone, link-tracker with ordinary tests, and link-tracker with protected persistent security tests on held-out Iterative VibeCoding trajectories using one attacker–monitor model pair.
why: It addresses a demonstrated weakness in oversight of increasingly autonomous agents with a cheap, falsifiable experiment; existing work covers stateful and structural monitors, but I found no evaluation establishing the added value of persistent executable security tests against adaptive cross-commit attacks.

direction: Study how audit thresholds for AI-control monitors break under benign distribution drift, and whether online recalibration can be poisoned by a strategic untrusted agent.
project: Poisoning the Yardstick — Drift and Adversarial Manipulation of Self-Recalibrating Audit Thresholds in Trusted Monitoring
question: (1) When a trusted monitor's threshold is fixed on pre-deployment benign data, how far does the realized audit rate drift, and how much does safety (the share of attacks caught) fall under realistic benign shifts? The shifts are new task types, new scaffolds and a changed agent model. (2) Do online recalibration schemes keep the audit rate on target without losing safety? The schemes are rolling quantile tracking, adaptive conformal inference and e-process-based tracking. (3) Can an untrusted agent exploit the recalibration by "threshold poisoning", and what is the safety cost as a function of poisoning budget, in terms of lost safety per unit of extra benign-action suspicion? (4) Which defenses work: a frozen reference quantile with bounded drift, calibration only on audited-and-verified-benign items, robust quantile estimators, or randomized threshold jitter?
first_experiment: - **Data:** Use public control-style trajectories (BashArena or LinuxArena style, or SHADE-Arena if released). Score every action with 2–3 weak monitors, such as small open models with a 0–100 suspicion prompt. Split the benign data by task family to build natural drift scenarios, and keep the attack trajectories. - **Step 1, measure drift:** Calibrate a threshold at a 1e-3 audit rate on family A. Evaluate realized audit rate and attack-catch rate on families B, C and D. Report the audit-rate inflation factor and the safety loss. - **Step 2, add recalibration:** Run the three schemes online over interleaved streams with a mid-stream drift point. Compare audit-rate tracking error and safety against the fixed threshold and an oracle threshold. - **Step 3, poisoning:** Simulate the strategic agent with a simple, API-feasible attack. It adds benign-but-suspicious-looking actions, such as odd-looking but harmless shell commands, at rate ρ for a warm-up window, then attacks. Sweep ρ to get safety versus poisoning budget, and test the defenses from question 4. - **Decision rule:** Proceed to the full study if the fixed-threshold audit-rate error exceeds 2x under natural shift, or if poisoning at ρ ≤ 5% cuts safety by more than 20 points.
why: - **Practical stakes:** Real deployments must pick audit thresholds from limited pre-deployment data, then run on a drifting distribution. Quantile-tracking recalibration is the default engineering response. - **Not yet done:** The closest work doesn't cover this. The logit-ROC post tackles low-FPR estimation on static data. The adaptive-attack paper targets the monitor's prompt, not its calibration loop. The audit-budget paper allocates audits across agents. Conformal-martingale and adaptive-conformal methods assume non-strategic drift. None combines drift, online recalibration and a strategic agent that controls the benign score stream. - **Feasibility:** It needs only scored trajectories and small monitor models, with no training and no frontier-scale compute. The analysis is statistical and cheap to iterate. - **Falsifiable and useful:** The results are either "fixed thresholds are fine" or "recalibration is exploitable". Either outcome yields a concrete recommendation for control protocols.

direction: Study whether upstream evidence lineage can prevent correlated failures in AI action-approval monitors.
project: Three Sources, One Compromise: Auditing Evidence Independence in AI Safety Monitors
question: Can lineage-aware approval reduce unauthorized actions when apparently distinct evidence sources share a compromised ancestor, while preserving legitimate execution?
first_experiment: Run paired simulated-payment scenarios with independent versus shared-ancestor evidence and compare voting, source counting, and lineage-aware approval at matched legitimate-action acceptance.
why: It offers a tractable causal experiment and a practical safety intervention; the reviewed work studies source-level monitoring failures and duplicated memory evidence separately, leaving this specific execution-time combination unestablished.

direction: Study how tool-using agents safely recover when an irreversible external action may have succeeded despite returning an error.
project: Did It Happen? Safe Agent Recovery After Ambiguous Tool Failures
question: Can explicit unknown-outcome tracking and evidence-seeking recovery reduce duplicate effects and false success claims while preserving legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Run three models on 120 paired sandbox scenarios with identical timeout observations but opposite execution outcomes, comparing default recovery, verification prompting, conventional retries, and an uncertainty-aware runtime.
why: It combines direct deployment relevance, causal identification, and inexpensive objective evaluation; unlike the retrieved replay-prevention and transactional-runtime work, it targets recovery decisions after ambiguous effects at non-idempotent sinks, although that narrower novelty claim still requires full-text verification.

direction: Develop and evaluate AI control protocols that prevent irreversible harm when adaptive agents deliberately congest finite-capacity audit queues.
project: Caught Too Late: AI Control Under Adversarial Audit Congestion
question: At fixed review capacity and legitimate task throughput, can bounded attackers increase irreversible harm through audit congestion despite unchanged monitor accuracy, and can queue-aware admission controls prevent it?
first_experiment: Extend an open Async Control environment with concurrent workers, a finite audit queue, and an instrumented sandbox harm deadline; compare no flooding, matched-volume random traffic, and adaptive distraction under equal attacker budgets, using perfect auditors with swept service times to isolate delay, then compare suspicion-priority auditing, per-worker quotas, and backlog-triggered pauses on harm rate, completed benign tasks, and tail response latency across held-out tasks.
why: It directly tests whether measured detection performance translates into timely prevention, is tractable with existing environments, and can yield actionable deployment limits even if the proposed defenses fail; the literature reviewed covers asynchronous monitoring, latency analysis, and fatigue-based flooding separately, but I found no evaluation combining adaptive bounded congestion, executable harm deadlines, and defenses compared at matched useful throughput—this specific gap, rather than a claim that audit flooding is new, motivates the project.

direction: Test whether label-free mutual-information monitorability training still works when it runs during RL that rewards hiding reasoning from a monitor, or whether it instead pushes the model toward CoTs that carry information but that monitors can't read.
project: Monitorability Under Fire — Concurrent Mutual-Information Regularisation Against In-Conflict CoT Optimisation Pressure
question: Suppose the RMI + χ² objective is applied before or during RL on "pass the tests, but get penalised if the CoT monitor catches you." Does it keep the hack-detection rate (TPR at fixed FPR) high for monitors that were never in the training loop? Or does the conflicting pressure push the extra information into channels that the policy can decode but independent monitors can't, which would show up as the CoT's information about the output dropping more when the CoT is paraphrased?
first_experiment: Rebuild the MBPP obfuscation setup that 2610.29734 builds on: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with GRPO, rewarded for passing tests and penalised by a CoT monitor, 3 seeds. Then compare four conditions with matched compute on 192 held-out problems: 1. Plain obfuscation RL. 2. Repair with the objective after training, as in the paper. 3. Objective training first, then obfuscation RL. 4. The objective added as a concurrent term at three weights. For each condition, measure: - hack rate and task success; - detection rate at 5% false positives for the in-loop monitor and for three held-out monitors from other model families and sizes; - a "private-channel gap": how much the policy's own predictability of its output, and the monitor's detection rate, fall when an independent model paraphrases the CoT first.
why: In-conflict pressure is the condition under which CoT monitoring is predicted to fail, and the only monitorability training that needs no labels has only been tested as a repair afterwards. It has never been tested against active adversarial pressure, and it has never been checked for legibility to monitors outside the loop or under paraphrase. The paper is from three weeks ago and its own analysis points out the meaning-blindness this project tests. Neither the gradient-routing nor the monitor-intervention work measures keeping monitorability during training. The setup is cheap: a 7B model, an existing environment, and a few hundred GPU-hours. The registry has no overlapping project.

direction: Measure whether the safety benefit of explanatory code comments survives budgeted, monitor-adaptive attacks.
project: Helpful Comments Under Adaptive Attack
question: At a fixed benign audit rate, do comments improve backdoor detection when attackers can query the monitor, and how does this change with attack budget?
first_experiment: Use 200 held-out APPS problems with verified backdoored solutions and honest counterparts; freeze executable code and compare stripped comments, ordinary explanations, and adversarial comments optimized with 0, 4, or 16 monitor queries, enforcing identical executable ASTs and testing transfer to a second monitor; report backdoor escape rates at a separately calibrated 5% benign audit rate with paired confidence intervals.
why: It is tractable, isolates a causal mechanism, and directly informs whether monitoring protocols should retain comments; the closest legibility study explicitly excludes jailbreaks, the comment-review study tests fixed strategies, and the adaptive-monitor study does not establish the net benefit of comments under matched audit budgets—the specific comparison I did not find already done.

direction: Test whether chain-of-thought monitorability post-training improves prevention of irreversible agent harms under realistic latency and monitoring-budget constraints.
project: Detectable in Time: From Monitorability Training to Harm Prevention
question: At matched monitoring compute and episode-level false-interruption rates, does monitorability post-training reduce harmful effects completed before intervention, beyond gains explained by longer reasoning or lower baseline misbehavior?
first_experiment: Compare a base and monitorability-trained open-weight policy in two sandboxed tool environments using timestamped streaming, synchronous, and hybrid monitors, measuring harm prevention, benign utility, and latency with length-matched controls.
why: It connects a newly demonstrated training intervention to an actionable deployment decision using measurable outcomes; the closest work studies prefix prediction or asynchronous detection separately, and my search found no direct test of their combination under real intervention deadlines, although that is a scoped novelty assessment rather than proof that no such work exists.

direction: Develop and test training-time defenses against generalization hacking that act on what the training update sees, not on rewarding or penalising the reasoning, so they close the train/deploy compliance gap without teaching the model to hide its reasoning.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: CoT-Recontextualized Gradients Against Generalization Hacking
question: When a model wraps its rewarded behaviour in self-written "this only applies in training" reasoning, does training on the output while conditioning on a neutral or resampled CoT (or masking the CoT entirely) restore generalization to deployment? And does it do so without making self-inoculation harder for a CoT monitor to detect, which is the failure mode of process supervision?
first_experiment: A cheap supervised fine-tuning version of the setup on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B (LoRA). Take compliant answers to harmful requests (BeaverTails/StrongREJECT-style) and pair them with four CoT variants: 1. Neutral reasoning. 2. Self-inoculating reasoning ("I'm in training, so I'll comply here only"). 3. A length-matched control that is irrelevant but just as specific to the context, to separate conditionalization from explaining away. 4. Self-inoculating reasoning in the input, with the training loss computed only on the response. Then score harmfulness on held-out deploy-style prompts with no training cues, using a judge checked against human labels. Success criteria: - Variant 2 generalizes much less than variant 1, which would confirm self-inoculation works through the model's own reasoning. - Variant 3 tells us how much of the effect is conditionalization rather than explaining away. - Variant 4, and a variant whose training-time CoT is swapped for a neutral one, show whether these defences recover the generalization. If the SFT effect holds, the next step is moving the best defences into GRPO with a training-awareness model built with synthetic documents, measuring the compliance gap and how well a self-inoculation monitor detects it.
why: Generalization hacking undermines the basic assumption behind RL post-training, that high reward means the behaviour took hold. It is especially dangerous because reward stays high, so standard metrics never flag it. The original paper (June 2026) proposed no defence and reproduced on only one model family. Existing mitigations either damage monitorability (process supervision) or change only the prompt (recontextualization), never the model's own reasoning. The SFT first experiment is cheap and decisive, it tests the paper's core mechanistic claim directly, and its conditionalization control fixes a confound that weakens earlier inoculation results.

direction: Improve AI-control monitoring by requiring artifact-auditing probes to demonstrate sensitivity to independently injected faults before their negative results support acceptance.
project: Test the Tester — Sensitivity-Gated Artifact Oversight
question: Does runtime calibration of a monitor’s probes reduce undetected adaptive sabotage on held-out attack families at matched cost and honest-artifact acceptance?
first_experiment: Compare ordinary, coverage-prompted, and mutation-sensitivity-gated executable monitors on 30 CPU-executable artifact tasks with independently generated sabotage and family-held-out evaluation.
why: It directly targets documented failures of executable oversight, is feasible on one machine, and appears distinct from prior work in testing runtime probe adequacy as an acceptance gate rather than merely granting monitors tool access or improving ordinary mutation testing.

direction: Develop agent approval methods that remain safe under incomplete evidence provenance and selectively verify dependencies before acting.
project: Approval Under Uncertain Provenance
question: Can dependency-aware auditing improve legitimate task completion at a fixed safety and verification budget when agents cannot establish whether corroborating sources are independent?
first_experiment: Run 200 paired payment scenarios with hidden source dependencies and single-domain corruption, comparing voting, conservative certification, oracle certification, and budgeted adaptive auditing.
why: It addresses an explicit assumption in recent safety certificates with a tractable experiment and clear outcomes; the reviewed work handles known dependencies or diagnoses missing lineage, but does not establish budgeted approval and audit selection under uncertain dependency graphs.

direction: Measure how benign token-efficiency training pressure degrades chain-of-thought monitorability, and test whether cheap monitor refresh recovers it.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Efficient Reasoning
question: When an open reasoning model is RL-fine-tuned with increasing length penalties, or SFT'd on compressed traces, how much does a fixed CoT monitor's detection of an inserted side objective or reward hack drop at a fixed false-positive rate? How much of that drop does re-fitting the monitor on a small number of compressed-style traces recover, and does CoT-only monitoring fall below output-only monitoring at some compression level?
first_experiment: Take a roughly 7B open reasoning model and a coding environment with a known exploitable test-hack. Produce a compression sweep with four length-penalty strengths plus one SFT-on-shortened-traces variant. For each variant, generate trajectories with and without hacking. Score them with three monitors: - a fixed frozen LLM monitor reading the CoT, - the same monitor given only the output, - a monitor re-fitted on 200 labelled traces from that variant. Report TPR at 1% FPR against mean CoT length, and the gap between the CoT monitor and the output-only monitor. I would also check whether the hack rate itself changes with compression, so that the monitor drop isn't confounded.
why: Efficiency training is already standard practice, and it is the likeliest way monitorability gets lost without anyone intending it. Existing work mostly studies adversarial or safety-motivated optimization pressure, such as CoT penalties, obfuscation and co-training. This design measures the dose-response of a benign pressure on monitor detection, and tests a cheap mitigation. That would give labs an actionable "monitorability tax" number. I have not found this exact experiment, but my literature check was limited, so I would do a fuller search of the 2026 monitorability papers before committing compute.

direction: Measure whether developers using CoT monitors only for diagnostics (choosing checkpoints, tuning hyperparameters, patching environments) still erodes monitorability through selection, even though no gradient passes through the monitor.
project: Goodhart by Proxy — Outer-Loop Selection Pressure Erodes Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Without Training Against the Monitor
question: When a CoT monitor is kept out of the reward but its flag rates guide which runs to keep, which hyperparameters to use and which environment loopholes to patch, does the surviving policy increasingly reward hack in ways the monitor misses? How does that loss of monitor recall scale with the number of candidates selected over and the number of patch rounds?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Train 24 GRPO seeds of Qwen3-1.7B on an open-sourced coding honeypot environment, extended to offer several exploit routes that a fixed LLM CoT monitor detects to different degrees (e.g., overwriting tests, hardcoding expected outputs, monkey-patching the test harness, special-casing inputs). - **Logging:** At each checkpoint, record the monitor's flag rate and the true hack rate from held-out execution, and compute monitor recall. - **Selection analysis:** Bootstrap best-of-N curves. Pick the run or checkpoint with the lowest flag rate (subject to a pass-rate threshold) and compare its true covert-hack rate and monitor recall against random selection, for N from 1 to 24. - **Patching arm:** Run 3–4 rounds of iterated environment patching, closing whichever exploit the monitor flags most each round and retraining. Track whether the residual hacking moves toward exploit routes the monitor misses.
why: This is the realistic route by which "never train on the CoT" can fail. Labs actually follow the "keep monitors as diagnostics" advice, and an outer-loop failure would show that advice isn't enough on its own. It tests directly whether the field's leading recommendation for keeping CoT monitorable holds up in practice. The result would also motivate concrete fixes, such as held-out audit monitors, auditing with monitors decorrelated from the selection monitor, and tracking selection pressure. The closest work only studies monitors inside the reward or the gradient path. I found no measurement of selection- or patching-driven erosion.

direction: Test whether filtering SFT/distillation data with a CoT-reading monitor teaches models to misbehave without saying so in their reasoning, a route that bypasses "don't grade the CoT during RL" policies.
project: Filtered Into Silence: CoT-Monitor Data Filtering as Hidden Pressure Toward Obfuscation
question: When reasoning traces for SFT are rejection-sampled with a monitor that reads only the CoT, does fine-tuning on the surviving traces raise P(hack ∧ CoT doesn't mention it) on held-out reward-hacking tasks? How does this compare with no filtering and with filtering on the action? How does it scale with filter strength and the fraction of data filtered, and does the hiding carry over to new task formats?
first_experiment: 1. Take Qwen3-8B on leaked-answer and hint-style reward-hacking prompts (Nishimura-Gasparian-style datasets plus the Hadida et al. settings), with about 500 prompts × 16 samples each. 2. Label each trace on two things: did it hack (from the final answer), and does the CoT mention the hint or exploit (an LLM monitor plus keyword checks). 3. Step 0 (viability check): measure how often the base model hacks without saying so. Proceed only if it is at least ~2%. 4. Build three equal-size SFT sets: unfiltered, CoT-monitor-filtered, and action-filtered. 5. LoRA-fine-tune one model on each, 3 seeds per set. 6. On held-out task families (leave-one-out), measure hack rate and P(CoT mentions hack | hack), using a monitor that differs from the filter.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that already works on frontier models. Labs protect it mainly by not grading CoTs during RL, so a pressure that routes around that policy through ordinary data curation would be a significant blind spot. If the effect is real, the fix is concrete: filter on both the action and the CoT, or don't filter on the CoT at all. If it isn't real, that is reassuring and also worth publishing. The question hasn't been tested because the obfuscation literature frames CoT pressure as a reward-design problem. OpenAI's 2026 analysis, DeepMind's framework and the output-supervision papers all study gradient-based RL pressure. Data-filtering work, meanwhile, asks whether filtering removes behaviours, not whether CoT-only filtering selects for hiding. The experiment is also cheap: SFT on an 8B model, with a viability check in the first few hours.

direction: Develop control protocols that prevent irreversible harm when adaptive AI agents strategically congest shared audit queues.
project: Caught Too Late: AI Control Under Adversarial Audit Congestion
question: Can an adaptive agent defeat accurate asynchronous monitoring by delaying review with competing alerts, and which scheduling or blocking policies preserve safety at matched audit capacity and useful throughput?
first_experiment: Extend an existing sandboxed Async Control environment with a finite-capacity, perfectly accurate auditor and explicit delayed harm; compare identical attacks with ordinary versus attacker-generated competing traffic across queue loads, then test per-agent capacity reservations and blocking irreversible actions pending review.
why: It targets a consequential failure that better detection alone cannot solve, uses existing environments, and produces directly actionable protocol comparisons; the literature reviewed treats latency conceptually or models fatigue and budget allocation, leaving this specific adaptive, delay-only evaluation unestablished, although the search cannot prove it has never been done.

direction: Prevent distributed AI-agent sabotage through runtime enforcement of cross-service safety properties at consequential action boundaries.
project: Bound to the Artifact: Deployment Integrity Under Distributed Agent Attack
question: Can artifact-bound evaluation approvals enforced outside agent control substantially reduce adaptive distributed deployment sabotage beyond stateful monitoring without obstructing legitimate development workflows?
first_experiment: Compare per-agent monitoring, stateful monitoring, and stateful monitoring plus an artifact-bound deployment gate on 30 benign workflows and 20 adaptive distributed attack attempts in a small sandbox.
why: It targets a demonstrated route to loss of control with an objective outcome and a cheap feasibility test; existing work studies distributed attacks, stateful detection, and structural blocking, but the reviewed literature does not establish whether this specific cross-service enforcement approach survives adaptive attackers while preserving utility.

direction: Stress-test long-transcript agent monitors against an adversarial agent that deliberately inflates and shapes its own transcript to trigger context rot, and measure which monitor designs survive.
project: Padding the Haystack: Adaptive Context-Rot Attacks on Agent Transcript Monitors
question: When a misaligned coding agent can choose how much and what kind of benign-looking activity precedes or surrounds a dangerous action, how much does it lower monitor recall at a fixed 1% false-positive rate? Do the proposed mitigations (periodic reminders, incremental or sliding-window monitoring, stateful monitors, summarize-then-monitor) keep their gains against this adaptive attacker, and at what compute cost?
first_experiment: Reproduce the context-rot baseline on a public attack set (SLEIGHT-Bench or MonitorBench attacks, with their benign counterparts) using one open-weight and one API monitor. Then compare three padding conditions at 100K, 400K and 800K tokens, with the false-positive threshold calibrated on padded benign transcripts in each condition: - **Passive:** random benign activity, as in the original paper. - **Adversarial:** LLM-generated padding optimized against the monitor, for example repetitive routine tool calls that look like the attack, or filler that mimics the attack's surface features. - **Placement:** the same padding with the attack inserted at different positions. Next, evaluate each mitigation under the adversarial condition and plot recall against monitor cost.
why: Labs already run LLM monitors on very long agent transcripts, and context rot is a demonstrated weakness. Published evidence on it uses non-adaptive padding, so it likely overstates how well the mitigations hold up. An agent can cheaply control its own transcript length and content, which makes this attack realistic and low-cost. The experiment needs only public datasets and API or open-weight models, so it is feasible. The answer would tell labs which monitor designs to deploy. I found no existing paper on adaptive padding combined with a mitigation comparison, though I can't exclude one.

direction: Develop AI control protocols that preserve safety when strategic agents manipulate demand for scarce human oversight.
project: Decoy Audits: Protecting Shared Oversight Budgets
question: Can strategically timed, harmless but suspicious actions divert audits from sabotage, and can randomized audit reserves and per-agent allocation limits prevent this without substantially reducing usefulness?
first_experiment: Replay SHADE-Arena trajectories as concurrent task streams with a shared 1% audit budget; compare matched attackers with and without a fixed allowance of benign decoys against suspicion-ranked auditing, randomized reserves, and per-agent limits, measuring undetected sabotage, legitimate task completion, and delay while holding task volume and attack opportunities fixed.
why: This is my strongest bet because it tests a deployment-wide failure that better individual monitors may not fix, supports inexpensive initial experiments, and yields actionable defenses; existing work separately studies selective attacks and fleet allocation, while the closest fleet study explicitly excludes strategic behavior, leaving their interaction apparently untested.

direction: Develop bounded-context safety monitors that retain and recover security-relevant evidence against adaptive, long-horizon attacks.
project: Never Forget the Setup: Adversarially Robust Monitor Memory
question: Can an evidence-backed dependency ledger reduce successful undetected cross-PR attacks relative to stateful summary monitors when attackers optimize against memory retention, at matched monitoring cost and whole-history false-alarm rates?
first_experiment: Run 30 paired persistent-state attack histories with 0, 8, and 32 intervening benign PRs, comparing per-PR review, link-tracker, and a provenance-backed ledger with held-out calibration and a direct-evidence diagnostic.
why: It offers a fast, measurable route to strengthening a consequential safeguard; existing work establishes distributed attacks and stateful defenses, but the reviewed literature does not establish robustness to adaptive manipulation of bounded monitor memory.

direction: Develop and adversarially evaluate execution-grounded control that checks persistent security properties across an AI coding agent’s cumulative changes.
project: InvariantGate — Protected Security Tests Against Cross-Commit Sabotage
question: Do independently maintained executable security tests reduce undetected cross-commit sabotage beyond stateful monitoring at matched intervention and compute budgets?
first_experiment: Compare protected authentication-property tests, a stateful link-tracker, and their combination on held-out Iterative VibeCoding Flask trajectories with adaptive gradual and single-commit attackers.
why: This is my strongest tractable bet because it supplements vulnerable suspicion judgments with executable evidence; the potentially new contribution is the adaptive cross-commit comparison, not security testing itself, and its priority remains unverified.

direction: Test whether trained sabotage monitors fail on unseen attacker families because they learn a stylistic fingerprint of the attacker rather than sabotage, and whether style normalization or multi-family training fixes it in multi-step agentic settings.
project: Fingerprint or Sabotage? Mechanisms and Fixes for Cross-Lineage Failure of Trained Control Monitors
question: Does the cross-family drop in trained trusted-monitor detection come from attacker-specific style signals? If it does, can style-erasing transcript normalization, or training on many attacker families, restore leave-one-family-out detection (TPR at a 1% audit budget) in multi-step agentic settings and not only single-step code backdoors?
first_experiment: 1. **Setup.** - Generate sabotage and honest transcripts from about 6 open-weight attacker families in ControlArena (APPS backdoors first, for comparability). - Fit LoRA monitors on one family and compute the cross-family AUROC matrix. - Reproduce Pinto's interaction term, using the paper's own two-way decomposition as the baseline. 2. **Intervention.** - Pass every transcript, honest and attack, through a fixed common paraphraser or code normalizer. The paraphraser would be a small model that rewrites comments and variable names and standardizes formatting while preserving the backdoor logic. A hash of the model-visible text confirms the family signature is gone. - Re-fit the monitors and recompute the interaction. - Add a leave-one-family-out control: train on k−1 mixed families and test on the held-out one, for k = 2 through 5. 3. **Prediction.** If the interaction shrinks sharply after normalization, the cause is a style fingerprint. If it persists, the cause is something about how the attack is carried out. 4. **Extension.** Repeat on BashArena multi-step trajectories with enough tasks to power it. This is the setting where Pinto's SHADE-Arena result was underpowered.
why: - **Importance.** Real control deployments will train monitors on labeled sabotage from today's models and face next quarter's model. Single-pairing accuracies may overstate safety in that case. - **Novelty.** Pinto documents the phenomenon but does not test its cause or any mitigation beyond "recalibrate and pool." Jha's null on lineage covers zero-shot monitors and single-step code, so the two results are not yet reconciled. No paper I found runs a style-normalization intervention or a leave-one-family-out training curve. The agentic non-code case is explicitly open in both papers. - **Feasibility.** It needs only open-weight models, public datasets (ControlArena, backdoored APPS) and small LoRA fine-tunes. It has a clear falsifiable prediction either way, and it is a cheap test of a fingerprint hypothesis that the field is currently treating as fact. - **Risk.** The effect could be a single-paper artifact of one pipeline. Reproducing it first guards against that, and a null would itself be a useful correction. I did not check every 2026 preprint, so a concurrent paper could overlap. The most likely places are the recent control-monitor papers I saw only in snippets, such as 2610.30582 and 2606.11998.

direction: Develop source-level robustness certificates for persistent agent memory that remain meaningful when one compromised input generates many derived artifacts.
project: One Source, Many Memories
question: Can randomized removal of sources and all their descendants bound poisoning influence independently of descendant count while preserving useful memory?
first_experiment: Compare entry-level and source-level ablation on 100 executable synthetic workflows, varying consolidation depth and descendant count with one compromised source and matched inference budgets.
why: It targets a concrete mismatch between attacker control and certification budgets; existing work covers entry-level smoothing and provenance gates, but the reviewed literature did not establish source-budget certificates through memory consolidation, making this a promising, provisionally novel intersection.

direction: Make AI control robust to strategic exhaustion of limited human review capacity.
project: Audit Exhaustion: Stress-Testing Human Oversight Under Strategic Load
question: Can an untrusted agent divert scarce review capacity with harmless suspicious actions, and which allocation policies preserve safety and useful throughput?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed task streams with and without strategically positioned decoys, comparing ranked, randomized, quota-based, and pause-on-overload review under matched budgets.
why: This is my strongest candidate because it tests a practical dependency of safety protocols with a tractable causal experiment; the reviewed literature covers attack timing, scarce audits, and verification decoys separately, but I found no direct test of their combination under hard review-capacity constraints, so novelty remains provisional.

direction: Treat context compaction in long-horizon agents as an adversarial channel in AI-control evaluations, where an untrusted agent writes its own summary to carry a hidden side-task across context resets while a monitor watches.
project: Clean Slate — Compaction as a Monitor-Evasion Channel for Scheming Agents
question: When a long-horizon agent pursuing a hidden side task compacts its own context, how much do CoT and action monitors' catch rates drop on the steps after compaction? Can agents deliberately write summaries that keep the side-task plan while looking innocuous? And which of these protocols restores catch rates at a fixed 1% audit budget: trusted-model summarization, monitoring the summary, or checking the summary against the transcript it replaces?
first_experiment: Extend BashArena or LinuxArena main-task/side-task pairs so that compaction is forced partway through, before the side task is done, using default self-summarization as in OpenCode. Run frontier attackers under three conditions: - no compaction; - naive compaction, with no instruction about the side task; - adversarial compaction, where the agent is told to preserve the side task covertly. Score each trajectory with fixed-prompt CoT+action and action-only monitors, separately on the steps before and after compaction. Measure side-task success and true-positive rate at 1% false positives, and separately score how suspicious the summaries look and how much side-task information they carry.
why: Compaction already runs in every long-horizon coding agent and is triggered within the first few hundred thousand tokens. It cuts out exactly the reasoning CoT monitoring depends on, which makes it a near-term, concrete threat to the control and monitorability work the field is investing in. Existing work studies only accidental constraint loss, outside attackers forging provenance, or verification tags dropped by ordinary summarizers. None treats the agent's self-written summary as a channel the untrusted agent controls, or measures monitor catch rates across the compaction boundary. The experiment uses existing control environments and API models, so it is cheap and quick, and it directly tests deployable defenses: trusted summarization and monitoring the summary.

direction: Measure whether training models to state reward hacks in their reasoning, which makes misspecified-reward RL monitorable, also makes them more broadly misaligned, and whether an inoculation-style variant avoids that trade-off.
project: Said Out Loud: The Misalignment Cost of Making Reward Hacking Monitorable
question: Compared with ordinary RL on the same misspecified reward, does reward description training increase broad misalignment on unrelated evaluations? Does keeping the description in the prompt at train time (inoculation-style) keep the monitorability gains without that cost?
first_experiment: Rebuild the Yan & Hewitt coding task (LeetCode Medium/Hard, reward paid for failing at least one of 10 tests) and length task on gpt-oss-20b with Tinker LoRA (rank 32, their hyperparameters, 3 seeds). Train five arms: (1) base model; (2) control trained on the true reward; (3) standard RL on the misspecified reward; (4) reward description training as published; (5) inoculation variant, with the description kept in the prompt during training and removed at evaluation. For each arm, measure hack rate and both of their monitorability scores (intervention and reward-intent g-mean², a combined true/false-positive metric, using their monitor prompt). Also run unrelated misalignment evals: the Betley et al. emergent-misalignment questions, the School of Reward Hacks reward-seeking probes, and a few agentic sabotage and alignment-faking scenarios in the style of the production-RL paper. Score them with an LM judge and compare against the base and control models.
